needs.label: Direction
needs.blurb: Help me decide what to do next.

needs.label: Confidence
needs.blurb: Help me believe this is right for me.

needs.label: Effort
needs.blurb: Make the task easier to complete.

needs.label: Intervention
needs.blurb: Help me recover when I stall or hit a barrier.

signals.label: Declared
signals.blurb: What the customer explicitly tells you

signals.label: Connected
signals.blurb: What you already know from past interactions

signals.label: Inferred
signals.blurb: A probable need estimated from available signals

steps.label: Signals
steps.question: What do we know?
steps.detail: Use what people tell you, what you can connect and what you infer. Check the quality of the signal before acting on it.

steps.label: The need
steps.question: What’s really going on?
steps.detail: Explain the customer problem behind the behavior. A signal is evidence; the need is a hypothesis to check.

steps.label: Worth it?
steps.question: Does it earn the work?
steps.detail: Estimate eligible reach, the full cost and the return needed to make the idea worthwhile. Compare it with a simpler option.

steps.label: The response
steps.question: How will we help?
steps.detail: Choose content, an experience change, a sequence or recommendations that address the need. Use the lightest effective response.

steps.label: The moment
steps.question: Did it help?
steps.detail: Compare with the default, read the result for eligible people and decide what to keep, change or stop. The learning becomes the next signal.

pillars.label: Strategy & culture
pillars.question: Is personalization serving a clear purpose?
pillars.kicker: Set direction, earn support and invest where a different experience can help.

items.text: Do we connect personalization to specific customer needs and business goals?
items.example: Help new customers choose a suitable plan, then measure whether successful activation improves.
items.guidance: Choose a customer problem and the business outcome that solving it should improve.

items.text: Does a senior sponsor support the program with time and funding?
items.example: A sponsor agrees priorities, protects delivery capacity and helps resolve competing demands.
items.guidance: Name a sponsor and agree the time, budget and decisions needed for the next quarter.

items.text: Do we prioritize opportunities using eligible reach, likely value and full cost?
items.example: Estimate who qualifies, plausible incremental value, and the cost of content, delivery, testing and upkeep.
items.guidance: Compare reach, plausible return and full cost before committing to a separate experience.

items.text: Do we improve the default experience before adding unnecessary personalization?
items.example: Fix a confusing checkout for everyone before maintaining separate versions for small audiences.
items.guidance: Compare each idea with improving the default and choose the smallest change that addresses the need.

items.text: Do leaders use evidence to decide what to scale, change or stop?
items.example: A treatment that fails to beat the default is revised or retired, even when it was a senior stakeholder’s idea.
items.guidance: Agree that measured outcomes, including losses, should guide investment and scaling.

pillars.detail: Set direction, earn support and invest where a different experience can help.

pillars.label: People & skills
pillars.question: Can the team turn insight into a useful experience?
pillars.kicker: Make ownership clear and bring research, design, delivery and measurement skills together.

items.text: Is someone accountable for personalization across the customer journey?
items.example: One named owner coordinates priorities, decisions and maintenance across marketing, product and service.
items.guidance: Assign accountability for the program and clarify who decides priorities and resolves conflicts.

items.text: Can we research customer needs and distinguish evidence from assumptions?
items.example: Use interviews, feedback and behavior to check why customers hesitate rather than assuming intent from a page view.
items.guidance: Give the team access to research skills and a repeatable way to check customer-need hypotheses.

items.text: Can we design and write responses that address those needs?
items.example: Designers and content specialists can turn a fit concern into useful sizing guidance or relevant recommendations.
items.guidance: Identify who can translate a validated customer need into useful content or an experience change.

items.text: Do we have the technical and analytical skills to deliver and evaluate experiences?
items.example: The team can implement targeting and tracking, QA both versions and interpret a controlled test.
items.guidance: Identify skill gaps in implementation, quality assurance and experiment analysis, then assign support.

items.text: Do the people involved have time and a clear way to work together?
items.example: Research, design, engineering and analytics have agreed responsibilities and capacity for the same initiative.
items.guidance: Agree roles, handoffs and delivery time so personalization is not dependent on spare time alone.

pillars.detail: Make ownership clear and bring research, design, delivery and measurement skills together.

pillars.label: Data & tools
pillars.question: Can we recognize, respond and measure reliably?
pillars.kicker: Use trustworthy signals, connected delivery and measurement that supports a fair comparison.

items.text: Can we access useful signals and identify where they came from?
items.example: Separate a declared preference, connected order history and inferred interest; make uncertainty visible.
items.guidance: List the signals available for one customer situation, their source and the confidence you have in them.

items.text: Do we manage identity, consent, freshness and signal quality?
items.example: Keep uncertain identities on the default, respect permissions and expire outdated preferences.
items.guidance: Define identity confidence, permissions, freshness checks and fallbacks before activating a signal.

items.text: Can the relevant signal reach the channel in time to change the experience?
items.example: A saved preference reaches the website or messaging tool before the next eligible interaction.
items.guidance: Check the connection and timing between the source of a signal and the place you will use it.

items.text: Can our tools deliver targeting rules, a default and a safe rollback?
items.example: A response can be limited to eligible people, avoid conflicting treatments and be switched off safely.
items.guidance: Confirm eligibility, exclusions, default behavior and rollback in the tools you already have.

items.text: Can we reliably measure assignment, exposure and customer outcomes?
items.example: Keep treatment assignment and exposure records and connect them to outcomes without double counting.
items.guidance: Check that assignment, exposure, outcomes and guardrails can be measured for the eligible audience.

pillars.detail: Use trustworthy signals, connected delivery and measurement that supports a fair comparison.

pillars.label: Process & methodology
pillars.question: Do we have a repeatable way to test and improve?
pillars.kicker: Work through the five-step use-case framework, then turn results into better decisions.

items.text: Do we document the signal, customer need and proposed response as a testable hypothesis?
items.example: State what you know, what you infer and how the response should help compared with the default.
items.guidance: Use Signals, Need and Response to explain why this audience should receive a different experience.

items.text: Do we assess feasibility and define eligibility before building?
items.example: Check audience size, delivery effort and overlapping rules; decide who qualifies and what everyone else sees.
items.guidance: Work through reach, cost, return, eligibility and fallback before committing to implementation.

items.text: Do we use a consistent review, QA and launch process?
items.example: Check targeting, content, accessibility, consent, tracking and rollback before releasing either version.
items.guidance: Use a shared QA checklist and assign ownership for launch, maintenance and stopping the treatment.

items.text: Do we plan a fair comparison, success measures and decision criteria before launch?
items.example: Randomize eligible people against a control or holdout, agree metrics and guardrails, and plan enough observation to support a decision.
items.guidance: Define the control, eligible audience, primary outcome, guardrails and decision criteria before starting.

items.text: Do we read results for the right audience and carry learning into the next decision?
items.example: Compare treatment and control within eligible people, record uncertainty and decide what to keep, change or stop.
items.guidance: Record what worked, for whom and why, then use that evidence to revise the next hypothesis.

pillars.detail: Work through the five-step use-case framework, then turn results into better decisions.

levels.label: Beginner
levels.blurb: Start with one person’s need and one reliable signal. Build the foundations before adding more experiences.

levels.label: Aspiring
levels.blurb: Some foundations are in place. Work on your weakest pillar before expanding to more audiences.

levels.label: Progressive
levels.blurb: You can connect signals to useful responses in some places. Make the value case and learning loop more consistent.

levels.label: Strategic
levels.blurb: Most program foundations are repeatable. Close the remaining gaps and compare outcomes across your use cases.

levels.label: Transformative
levels.blurb: Your self-assessment suggests a repeatable practice across the four program pillars. Keep validating those answers with evidence and measured outcomes.

opportunities.title: A first-timer and a regular see the same homepage.
opportunities.summary: Help new people get oriented. Let regulars skip ahead.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Anonymous first-timers land on a homepage built for people who already know you, or regulars land on a brochure built for strangers. The session type is sitting right there. The layout does not change.
opportunities.whyItEarns: New vs returning is a coarse split, but it is honest and testable. Orient the new; shorten the path for the known. Hold out the default.
opportunities.confusion: A "Welcome back, FirstName" bar is not a different homepage.

signals.example: Completed orders, recognized visits, account state, and browser recognition.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Treat someone as a regular when completed orders > 1 and recognized visits > 2 in the previous 90 days. Treat someone as a first-timer when completed orders = 0 and recognized visits <= 1. Keep everyone else on the default until the evidence is clearer.

arms.low: Keep the default. A quiet "new here" vs "pick up where you left off" chip.
arms.medium: Swap the first module: orientation for new, resume for returning.
arms.high: Two first screens, same URL, with a way back to the other.

test.treatment: New vs returning first screen, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Randomize first-timers and regulars separately. Within each segment, compare the tailored homepage with the unchanged homepage. Do not combine the two segments into one average.
test.primaryMetric: First-session task start (search, PDP, signup) vs returning conversion.
test.guardrail: Returning bounce. Do not hide the catalog they came to browse.

pitfalls: Treating a cleared-cookie regular as new and wiping their path.
A first-timer experience that cannot reach the full catalog.
Personalizing on "returning" when the only signal is a marketing cookie.

opportunities.title: They said why they came. You showed the homepage.
opportunities.summary: Show them that next, not everything.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A new visitor names a job in a search box, a quiz, or a "what brings you here" prompt. The next screen ignores it and presents the average homepage.
opportunities.whyItEarns: The cost of specificity is low: they already typed the answer. Showing a narrower set is usually cheaper than making them hunt, and it is easy to test against the default.
opportunities.confusion: This is not "Hi, FirstName." It is taking the sentence they just gave you and changing what they see next.

signals.example: Onboarding quiz, search query, or "I'm here to…" picker.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Apply the goal-aware experience when the visitor explicitly selects a supported goal or submits a non-empty query that maps confidently to one path. Keep the default when they choose "explore," skip the prompt, or provide an answer that maps to several paths equally well.

arms.low: Keep the default page. Quietly boost matching modules in the existing layout.
arms.medium: A single banner or module that names the goal and offers the next step.
arms.high: Replace the first screen with a short path built around that goal.

test.control: Same homepage or category page for everyone.
test.treatment: Goal-aware first screen, with a holdout that still sees the default.
test.primaryMetric: Activation of the named task (start rate, not vanity clicks).
test.guardrail: Bounce and "back to browse." If people flee, you over-narrowed.

pitfalls: Treating a vague goal ("explore") as a mandate to hide the catalog.
No way to get back to the full experience.
Measuring page views instead of task completion.

opportunities.title: They searched for something specific. You showed bestsellers.
opportunities.summary: Put what they asked for first.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Query language is specific (a size, a job, a competitor) but merchandising still sorts by bestsellers. The customer has to filter their way back to what they asked for.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Search is one of the clearest places customers state their intent. Acting on that signal is more useful than adding personalized decoration elsewhere.
opportunities.confusion: Better search is personalization. You do not need a "personalization platform" to rank the right 12 products first.

signals.example: The query, filters, and spelling variants.
Past purchases or category affinity that should re-weight results.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Re-rank when the query contains a recognized product, job, or attribute and produces at least 12 relevant results. Use purchase history only for authenticated customers with at least two prior category interactions. Keep default ranking for ambiguous, navigational, or very broad queries.

arms.low: Keep the current layout, but explain the ranking: "Because you searched for waterproof hiking shoes, waterproof trail options appear first."
arms.medium: Re-rank the first page around the query and known affinity.
arms.high: A guided results template: matching items, a missing-filter prompt, and a related-need module.

test.treatment: Intent-weighted ranking for the same query.
test.primaryMetric: Search-to-product (or article) engagement, then conversion.
test.guardrail: Zero-result rate and filter usage. Spikes mean you hid too much.

pitfalls: Overfitting to last click and creating a filter bubble.
No holdout, so you never know if ranking actually paid.
Ignoring null searches, which are often the highest-intent misses.

opportunities.title: They filled in the quiz. Then the site forgot.
opportunities.summary: Use those answers on the next page and the next visit.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A preference center, sizing quiz, ICP form, or "tell us about your team" survey captured a clear need. The next pages, and the next visit, still treat them as unknown.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Declared data is usually one of the clearest signals available. Ignoring it teaches people that answering did not improve the experience.
opportunities.confusion: Collecting the data is not personalization. Using it on the next screen is.

signals.example: Quiz answers, role, team size, use case, constraints.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Apply the answers after the customer completes the quiz and all fields required for the treatment are present. Keep them active until the customer edits them or contradictory declared information appears. Do not personalize from an abandoned or partially completed quiz.

arms.low: Show a specific, editable recap: "You told us you're furnishing a small apartment, so compact sofas and storage beds appear first."
arms.medium: Homepage and email use the answers as the primary sort, with an edit path.
arms.high: A first-run experience assembled from the answers, then a save into the profile.

test.treatment: Answer-aware destination and follow-up.
test.primaryMetric: Time-to-first-value after the form.
test.guardrail: Form completion rate. If the follow-up feels like a trap, completions drop.

pitfalls: Asking 12 questions to power one module.
No edit or "this isn't me" control.
Storing answers in a tool that the site cannot read.

opportunities.title: Search came back with nothing they can use.
opportunities.summary: Show a close match for what they typed.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A specific query (SKU, size, job, misspelling) returns zero results or a junk page. High intent, no path. Most people leave rather than rewrite the query.
opportunities.whyItEarns: A null search is a clear signal that the current path failed. A close match, a synonym, or a "we don't have this, here's the nearest" is a different experience that is easy to test against the default.
opportunities.confusion: A prettier empty state is not recovery. This case repairs a failed query. "They filtered until there was nothing left." repairs a filter combination that removed every result.

signals.example: The query, zero-result flag, and any filters they had on.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger after the search engine returns zero usable results following normal spelling correction and synonym expansion. Preserve the original query and filters. Treat service errors, unavailable indexes, and unsupported characters as technical failures rather than intent-recovery opportunities.

arms.low: Keep the empty page. Add a close-match chip and a way to drop one filter.
arms.medium: Synonym and attribute recovery: show the nearest in-stock set, named as such.
arms.high: A guided recovery: nearest products, a notify-me, and a related-need module.

test.treatment: Intent-recovery results for the same query.
test.primaryMetric: Search-to-product after a null, then conversion.
test.guardrail: Bounce on the results page. If they still leave, you recovered the wrong thing.

pitfalls: Showing bestsellers that ignore the query.
No holdout, so you never know if recovery paid.
Hiding that you do not actually stock what they asked for.

opportunities.title: They want it. It's out of stock.
opportunities.summary: Show something in stock that fits, and a waitlist that actually writes back.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A PDP, a search hit, or a rec points at something you cannot sell today. Default is a grey button. No nearest size, no similar in-stock, no waitlist they can actually use.
opportunities.whyItEarns: High intent plus unavailability is a fork: recover to a substitute, capture the wait, or lose them to a competitor who has it.
opportunities.confusion: A notify-me form is not a substitute. Showing the next best in-stock item, with a reason, is.

signals.example: The product, size, or query they asked for.
Prior purchase of that line, or a saved size.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger when the selected variant is unavailable and the visitor has either attempted to add it or viewed the PDP at least twice. Rank substitutes only when they match the selected size or compatibility requirement, remain within 20% of the original price, and share the product's primary use.

arms.low: Keep the OOS page. A waitlist and one similar in-stock card.
arms.medium: Lead with in-stock alternatives that match the attribute they cared about.
arms.high: Substitute-first layout, waitlist, and a "we'll hold it" path if restock is near.

test.treatment: Substitute-and-wait recovery.
test.audienceReadout: Among visitors who met the out-of-stock rule, compare substitute engagement, alternative-item conversion, and waitlist joins with the default out-of-stock experience. Break results out by declared size, saved size, and inferred product interest.
test.primaryMetric: Conversion to an in-stock alternative, plus waitlist quality.
test.guardrail: Returns on the substitute. A bad swap is worse than a waitlist.

pitfalls: Pushing a more expensive substitute without saying so.
Waitlists that never fire.
Hiding OOS so search looks full, then failing at cart.

opportunities.title: They're ready to buy something new. You keep selling last time.
opportunities.summary: Let this visit lead. Don't trap them in what they already bought.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A known customer has compared products in a new category and added one to the cart. The cart and recommendations still push the last purchase instead of helping complete the new decision.
opportunities.whyItEarns: The session is telling you the job changed. Using history as a prior, not a prison, is where specificity pays.
opportunities.confusion: More recommendations is not more personalization. This case improves the current purchase decision. "A regular is looking for something new. You send them last year's path." redesigns the broader returning-customer experience.

signals.example: Purchase history plus repeated comparison or cart activity in a different category.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Require at least two completed purchases in the historical category, then at least two PDP views and one cart add in a different category during the current session. A single view in a new category is not enough to change the experience.

arms.low: Keep recs, but label them "from last time" and demote them below session matches.
arms.medium: Session-first recs, with a small "your usual" module.
arms.high: A split merchandising layout: "for this visit" vs "your staples", and a path to switch.

test.treatment: Session-need weighted recs for known buyers.
test.audienceReadout: Among known buyers who meet the category-shift rule, compare session-first recommendations with history-first recommendations. Report new-category purchase and staple repurchase separately.
test.primaryMetric: Completed purchase in the new category.
test.guardrail: Repeat-purchase rate of staples. Do not bury a familiar path that still matters.

pitfalls: Wiping history the moment someone browses a gift.
No language that explains the shift, so it feels random.
Applying the same rule to first-time buyers with thin history.

opportunities.title: They logged in to an empty screen, not what they came to do.
opportunities.summary: Make the first screen about what they said they wanted.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Signup or a "what will you use this for" question already happened. The empty state is still a feature parade instead of a first action built around that answer.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Activation personalization is a different first job, not a longer checklist. Role- and use-case-based first screens are how people reach value in minutes instead of a day.
opportunities.confusion: A personalized welcome tooltip is not a different first experience. This case chooses the right first action. "They signed up. The first screen still looks like someone else's demo." makes the example or proof feel relevant.

signals.example: Signup job, role, or "I'm here to…" answer.
Plan, invite source, or the page they came from.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Show the job-first empty state when the account has a declared use case, has not completed its first-value event, and the selected job is available on the current plan. Use the default empty state for "explore," conflicting answers, or accounts that already contain work.

arms.low: Keep the default empty state. One module that names the job they chose.
arms.medium: Reorder the first three actions around the stated job, with skip.
arms.high: A first-run assembled from the job, then a path back to the full product.

test.treatment: Job-first empty state for the same signup answers.
test.primaryMetric: First-value event in session one, then activation at day 7.
test.guardrail: Skip rate and time-to-full-product. If they cannot reach the rest, you over-narrowed.

pitfalls: Twelve-item checklists dressed as personalization.
No way back to the full product.
Treating "explore" as a mandate to hide navigation.

opportunities.title: A regular is looking for something new. You send them last year's path.
opportunities.summary: Ask: same as last time, or this?
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Reorder module, "continue the series", the beginner tour, last season's aisle: all correct for the old job. This session they searched a new category, invited a different role, or opened a different sport. History is a prior, not a prison.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Retention personalization that only replays the last order trains people to ignore you. A fork (usual path or the new one this session named) is the test.
opportunities.confusion: A "welcome back" with last year's merchandising is not recognition. This case changes the return path across visits. "They're ready to buy something new. You keep selling last time." focuses on recommendations during an active shopping session.

signals.example: Search or browse behavior that does not match the customer's established category, plan, or saved preference.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Define a regular as someone with completed orders > 1 or recognized visits > 2 in the previous 90 days. Require at least two meaningful views or one search plus one detail view in the new category before offering a new path. Keep the usual path visible.

arms.low: Keep the usual module. Add a chip for the new thread they just started.
arms.medium: Split the first screen: usual, and the new job this session.
arms.high: Lead with the new job, keep the usual one tap away, stop the old tour.

test.treatment: Session-aware fork, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Among regulars who meet the new-interest rule, compare the session-aware fork with the usual returning experience. Measure completion of the new job and any decline in habitual conversion separately.
test.primaryMetric: Completion of the new job (new category purchase, new feature used).
test.guardrail: Reorder or habitual conversion. Don't starve the path that still pays.

pitfalls: Wiping a loyal path because of one curious click.
The beginner tour on a three-year customer.
No way back to "the usual".

opportunities.title: They keep doing it the hard way.
opportunities.summary: Show the easier way while they're still doing it by hand.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A user exports a CSV every Friday, reorders by hunting, or copies a workflow by hand. A feature, plan, or integration would remove that repeated work. They have never been shown it at a moment when the benefit is obvious.
opportunities.whyItEarns: This is expansion with a conscience: you are not upselling a stranger, you are offering a shorter path through a job they already do.
opportunities.confusion: An "upgrade to Pro" banner on every page is not this. This is a prompt at the moment of the workaround.

signals.example: Repeated export, reorder, or manual steps that map to an unused feature.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger only after the same manual workaround occurs at least three times in 30 days, the mapped capability remains unused, and the user has permission to try it. Reset the count after adoption or dismissal.

arms.low: A one-line tip next to the workaround: "there's a faster way".
arms.medium: A contextual offer with a 30-second preview of the capability.
arms.high: A trial of the capability in-flow, with a clear way back.

test.control: No prompt, or the global upsell banner.
test.treatment: In-moment prompt tied to the workaround.
test.audienceReadout: Among accounts that met the repeated-workaround rule, compare the contextual prompt with no prompt. Track capability adoption and retained use, not just prompt clicks.
test.primaryMetric: Capability adoption, then expansion revenue or retained usage.
test.guardrail: Prompt dismiss rate and support tickets calling it spam.

pitfalls: Prompting on the first occurrence. Wait for a pattern.
Pitching a paid plan before showing the job-to-be-done.
No "already using a different tool for this" escape.

opportunities.title: The logos and quotes are for a different kind of company.
opportunities.summary: Put proof from companies like theirs on the first screen.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A 12-person studio lands on a page full of Fortune 500 logos. Or an enterprise buyer sees "for startups". Proof, examples, and pricing cues all misfire. They do not need a different product yet. They need to believe it is for them.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Confidence is the job of acquisition personalization. If the first screen argues with their identity, nothing downstream gets a fair test.
opportunities.confusion: Relevant proof is useful only when the segment is accurate and the change is understandable. A quiet industry cue is better than a page that rearranges itself without explanation.

signals.example: Firmographic match from CRM, a form field, authenticated account data, or a company-domain match.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Use declared or CRM firmographics when available. For an inferred segment, require two agreeing sources, such as company domain plus account-level browsing, before changing proof. IP alone can suggest a segment but should not qualify someone for the full treatment.

arms.low: Keep the page. Swap one proof module (logo row or quote) for their segment.
arms.medium: Headline, proof, and CTA framed for their size or industry.
arms.high: A full account-aware page with relevant use cases and a matching next step.

test.control: Default homepage or campaign landing page.
test.treatment: Segment-aware proof and framing.
test.audienceReadout: Evaluate declared, connected, and inferred segments separately. For the inferred segment, compare qualifying visitors who received matched proof with qualifying holdout visitors who saw the default proof, then monitor correction and "not my company" rates.
test.primaryMetric: Qualified demo or trial start.
test.guardrail: Mis-identified accounts. Always offer "not your company?"

pitfalls: Guessing industry from IP and being loudly wrong.
Hiding pricing from enterprises and frustrating them.
No holdout, so you never know if the swap moved pipeline.

opportunities.title: The ad made a promise the page doesn't keep.
opportunities.summary: Keep that promise on the page they land on.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: They clicked "waterproof trail runners, 20% off" or "SOC 2 for finance teams" and landed on a generic homepage. The landing experience fails to continue the specific promise that earned the visit.
opportunities.whyItEarns: You already paid for the intent. Continuity is cheaper than retargeting them because the page felt like a bait-and-switch.
opportunities.confusion: UTM-aware pages are personalization. They do not require a CDP. They require a landing template and the discipline to use it.

signals.example: Campaign, creative, keyword, or partner ID on the landing session.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Use message-matched content only when the campaign ID resolves to an active, approved promise and the landing-page variant supports the exact product, audience, and offer. Unknown parameters, expired offers, direct navigation, and brand search remain on the default page.

arms.low: A banner that restates the ad promise and points to the matching module.
arms.medium: Hero, proof, and primary SKU or offer match the creative.
arms.high: A dedicated template per campaign cluster, still tested against the default home.

test.treatment: Message-matched landing experience.
test.primaryMetric: Campaign conversion (purchase, lead, trial).
test.guardrail: Direct-nav and brand-search traffic. Don't "personalize" people who typed your name.

pitfalls: A unique page per ad that nobody can maintain.
Continuing the discount after the session if they didn't come for it.
Forgetting mobile creatives that promised a different product.

opportunities.title: An engineer landed on a page written for a buyer, or the reverse.
opportunities.summary: Show proof that matches who's actually looking.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Pages, docs, or security content show who they are. The homepage and CTA still speak to a generic "team". The practitioner wants how it works. The economic buyer wants risk and outcome. Mixing them stalls both.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Role is a confidence problem, not a decoration problem. Match proof and CTA to the job of the person in the session, and always offer the other path.
opportunities.confusion: Putting their job title in the headline is not the same as changing the proof.

signals.example: Known contact title from CRM, or pages they keep opening (docs vs pricing vs security).
Enrichment title, or two+ views of API / ROI / implementation.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Infer practitioner intent after at least two API, documentation, or implementation views in 14 days. Infer buyer intent after at least two pricing, security, or ROI views in 14 days. If the paths conflict, show the role switch instead of selecting a role.

arms.low: Keep the default. A quiet "for practitioners / for buyers" switch.
arms.medium: Swap the proof module and CTA; keep the rest.
arms.high: A first screen assembled around the role, with an obvious "not my job" escape.

test.treatment: Role-aware proof and CTA, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: For visitors who met a role-inference rule before assignment, compare role-aware proof with the generic page. Report practitioner and buyer outcomes separately, along with use of the role-correction switch.
test.primaryMetric: Qualified next step (docs start, demo, or pricing) by role.
test.guardrail: Wrong-role bounce. If engineers get a CFO page, you will see it.

pitfalls: Trusting enrichment title without a way to correct it.
Hiding pricing from practitioners who need it to champion.
One account, many roles, one cookie.

opportunities.title: They're browsing. Nothing says this is for people like them.
opportunities.summary: Put proof for people like them where they're looking.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Category, PDP, or pricing grid. Reviews, returns, "used by teams like yours" sit below the fold or on a different page. They are deciding whether this is even in the right neighborhood. The average proof is for someone else.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Confidence belongs where they are looking, not in a trust-badge strip. For example, a first-time parent browsing travel strollers could see a verified review from another parent who tested the stroller on public transit, plus the return policy beside it.
opportunities.confusion: A star rating is not proof for their size, job, or use. "People like you bought this" has to be true.

signals.example: Category or PDP views, no cart, plus a known or inferred use context.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Require at least two detail views within the same use context, such as compact travel products, plus one supporting behavior such as a relevant filter or comparison. Use cohort proof only when the referenced cohort has a verified attribute and enough completed purchases or reviews to support the claim.

arms.low: Keep the grid. Surface one relevant review or return line in the existing card.
arms.medium: Proof module on the category or PDP framed for their segment.
arms.high: Reorder the set and proof around the known need, such as travel strollers tested on public transit, with a way back to the full catalog.

test.treatment: In-place proof for the session's segment, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Among visitors who qualified for the same inferred use context, compare matched proof with generic proof. Track progression and "not relevant" interactions so a persuasive result is not hiding a bad inference.
test.primaryMetric: Add-to-cart or demo start from that listing.
test.guardrail: Wrong-segment complaints and "not for me" exits.

pitfalls: Inventing a "people like you" set from one pageview.
Hiding the catalog behind a segment story.
Using enterprise logos on a page a 12-person team is browsing.

opportunities.title: They keep opening pricing and never pick a plan.
opportunities.summary: Help them choose. Another comparison table won't.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Three, four, five visits to /pricing. No plan selected. The default comparison table does not answer the question they are stuck on, usually "which one is for us" or "what happens if we outgrow it".
opportunities.whyItEarns: Repeat pricing visits are a loud "help me choose" signal. A calculator, a recommended plan, or social proof for their size is a different experience that can be tested cleanly.
opportunities.confusion: A popup that says "wait, 20% off" is not direction. It is pressure. Direction looks like a recommended plan with a reason.

signals.example: Repeat pricing views, time on page, plan-toggle events, and return visits.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger after at least three pricing-page visits across two or more sessions in 14 days, or after two visits with a seat-count change and plan comparison, with no plan selected. Exclude current customers checking an invoice.

arms.low: No modal. A quiet "not sure? compare in two questions" link.
arms.medium: A recommended plan based on company size or stated seats, with an explanation.
arms.high: Interactive chooser plus a human "talk to us" for edge cases, still tested against the table.

test.treatment: Chooser or recommended-plan module for repeat visitors.
test.audienceReadout: Among visitors who met the pricing-consideration rule, compare the chooser with the static table. Measure plan selection and qualified trial or demo starts, then inspect recommendation overrides and wrong-plan support contacts.
test.primaryMetric: Plan select / trial start from pricing.
test.guardrail: Discount-seeking and support tickets about "wrong plan".

pitfalls: Leading with a discount because you can, not because they asked.
Recommending the most expensive plan by default.
No way to see all plans after a recommendation.

opportunities.title: They keep coming back to the same product. They still won't buy.
opportunities.summary: Answer what's stopping them. Don't just say buy again.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A handful of product or pricing views, no conversion. They are missing a reason to trust: returns, implementation, who it is for, what happens after pay. The page keeps shouting the same CTA.
opportunities.whyItEarns: At this point, the useful job is reassurance where the decision has stalled, not more personalized decoration.
opportunities.confusion: An exit discount trains people to wait. Relevant proof, clearer fit, and risk reduction address the decision they are actually making.

signals.example: Repeat PDP or pricing views, scroll depth, comparison behavior, and no purchase.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Require at least three views of the same product or plan across two sessions in 14 days, with at least one deep-scroll or comparison event and no cart, trial, or purchase. First-session repetition alone does not qualify.

arms.low: No popup. If a 25-person agency keeps returning to the same plan, surface the cancellation terms and a verified agency case study in the existing layout.
arms.medium: A sticky module answering the likely objection for this product or plan.
arms.high: A compare-and-decide layer (fit quiz, implementation snapshot, talk-to-expert) still tested vs default.

test.treatment: Reassurance module for repeat viewers.
test.audienceReadout: Among visitors who met the repeat-consideration rule, compare objection-specific reassurance with the unchanged page. Measure eventual conversion and track dismissals, discount use, and support contacts by inferred objection.
test.primaryMetric: Conversion on the viewed item or plan.
test.guardrail: Discount rate and margin. If the only thing that works is money off, you learned something else.

pitfalls: Firing on the first visit. Repeat means repeat.
Stacking chat, popup, and banner at once.
Social proof from a segment that is not them.

opportunities.title: The cart is full. They still won't pay.
opportunities.summary: Put delivery, returns, and a reason to trust next to pay.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Items are in the cart. The pause is not discovery. It is risk: shipping cost, arrival date, returns, payment trust. The cart still looks like a list of SKUs.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Proof belongs at the point of commit, not in a footer. For a customer ordering a sofa, show the delivery window, room-of-choice terms, and a verified review from another apartment customer beside the total.
opportunities.confusion: Another discount is not reassurance. Answering the actual doubt is.

signals.example: Cart contents, time-on-checkout, payment-method abandons, shipping estimator opens.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Show reassurance when an in-stock cart remains open for at least 60 seconds, the customer opens delivery or return details, or revisits the payment step without submitting. Route validation errors and payment failures to recovery instead of confidence messaging.

arms.low: Keep the cart. A single line for delivery and returns next to the total.
arms.medium: Proof at the pay button: arrival window, returns, a relevant review.
arms.high: Checkout that names the risk for this cart (oversize, preorder, international) and a way to proceed anyway.

test.treatment: Doubt-aware cart for the same items.
test.primaryMetric: Checkout completion.
test.guardrail: Discount rate. If the treatment only works with a coupon, you did not answer the fear.

pitfalls: A popup on the pay button.
Generic "trusted by thousands" that ignores this cart.
Surprising fees after the treatment promised a number.

opportunities.title: They signed up. The first screen still looks like someone else's demo.
opportunities.summary: Show an example that looks like their world, not a stock screenshot.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Account created. Dashboard, sample data, or "welcome to the platform" with stock examples from another industry or role. They cannot tell if this will work for them. Direction would give them a first job. Confidence is showing a result that looks like theirs.
opportunities.whyItEarns: The first session must make the product's value believable. A recruiter could see a sample candidate pipeline, while a support lead could see a sample queue with routing rules. Both are testable against the same blank slate.
opportunities.confusion: A product tour is not proof. This case makes the result feel credible and relevant. "They logged in to an empty screen, not what they came to do." chooses the first action they should take.

signals.example: Role, use case, or industry named at signup, and an empty or sample workspace.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Load a relevant example when the customer declared a supported role or use case, the workspace contains no customer data, and no first-value event has occurred. Use a blank start when they selected "start from scratch" or when no trustworthy example matches.

arms.low: Keep the empty state. Swap sample names and screenshots for their use case.
arms.medium: A first screen with one example result in their world, then the first action.
arms.high: Pre-built workspace or sample project for that role, skippable, with a way to start blank.

test.control: Generic empty state or sample data.
test.treatment: Use-case-aware first proof, with a holdout.
test.primaryMetric: First key action in-session (not tour completion).
test.guardrail: People who wanted a blank slate and felt the example was in the way.

pitfalls: Loading a noisy demo dataset they cannot delete.
Guessing the use case from email domain and being loudly wrong.
Calling the tour "personalized" because it used their first name.

opportunities.title: Renewal is coming. They've never seen what they got out of it.
opportunities.summary: Show them their own results before you send the invoice.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Ninety, sixty, thirty days out. Usage exists, or it doesn't, and the default is a generic "your plan renews" invoice. No outcomes, no seats used, no "this is what you shipped". They cannot say yes with a straight face.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Renewal is a confidence problem first. Proof of their own results is cheaper and more honest than a discount 10 days before the date.
opportunities.confusion: A win-back coupon on a healthy account is not reassurance. It trains them to wait.

signals.example: Renewal date, usage vs their baseline, outcomes the product can already name.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Show the value recap when renewal is within 30 days, the account has at least one complete billing period of usage, and every reported outcome can be traced to product data. Use a simple renewal notice when usage is too sparse or the outcome calculation is incomplete.

arms.low: A quiet usage recap in-product. No broad email campaign.
arms.medium: A "your year in this product" at the billing surface, with a human offer for high-value.
arms.high: Value-first renewal path: outcomes, then plan, then pay. Discount only if they ask.

test.treatment: Own-value recap before the paywall.
test.primaryMetric: Renewal rate and expansion at renewal, not email clicks.
test.guardrail: Discount rate. If the recap only works with money off, you did not show value.

pitfalls: Inventing ROI numbers they will not recognize.
Leading with a downgrade scare.
The same recap for a champion and an idle seat.

opportunities.title: They're considering more. The next plan still looks like a brochure.
opportunities.summary: Show proof from how they already use it, not a feature list.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Usage is healthy, or they viewed billing. The next plan is a generic grid: more seats, more logs, more "advanced". No proof from accounts like them, no picture of their own results on the next tier. They do not need a harder sell. They need to believe the jump is for them.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Expansion confidence is "this worked, the next step looks like that, for us". Feature lists are what you show strangers. Hold out the brochure against proof that uses their own usage.
opportunities.confusion: A usage meter that turns red is not proof. A verified example is: "A 30-person support team moved to this tier to automate ticket routing and add audit logs."

signals.example: Plan, usage relative to limits, billing-page views, and the role of the person in-session.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Qualify an account after two billing or upgrade views in 30 days, or when sustained usage exceeds 80% of a relevant limit for two weeks, provided the current workflow is healthy. A single billing visit does not establish expansion intent.

arms.low: Keep the grid. Add one relevant proof point, such as a 30-person support team using automated routing, or show the account's own usage recap.
arms.medium: Upgrade page framed with their results and a matching next plan.
arms.high: In-product, at the moment they need the next thing, with proof and a human for high-fit accounts.

test.treatment: Account-aware proof on the next plan, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Among accounts that met the expansion-consideration rule, compare account-aware proof with the standard upgrade page. Report upgrade starts, completed expansion, and 30-day adoption of the added capability.
test.primaryMetric: Expansion conversion of accounts that viewed the next plan.
test.guardrail: Trust. Invented ROI, or a scare about hitting the limit, should fail.

pitfalls: Inventing savings they will not recognize.
The same enterprise case study for a ten-person team.
Blocking the current plan to force the conversation.

opportunities.title: They landed in the wrong country, currency, or language.
opportunities.summary: Offer the right store. Always let them stay on this one.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: IP, browser language, or a .com default puts them in the wrong catalog. Prices in the wrong currency. Copy they cannot read. They have to hunt a flag icon before they can shop or sign up.
opportunities.whyItEarns: This is manners, not targeting. Detect, offer the match, and let them keep the default. Easy to hold out against the untranslated homepage.
opportunities.confusion: Auto-redirecting without a way back is how you hide the catalog they typed the URL for.

signals.example: IP country, browser language, current store, and currency behavior.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Offer a locale switch when IP country and browser language agree and both differ from the current store, or when the visitor changes currency twice. If location and language disagree, keep the current store and show only a quiet selector.

arms.low: A quiet bar: "Shop in £ / English?" with keep-this-site.
arms.medium: Offer the matching store first. One tap to stay on the current one.
arms.high: Route new sessions to the matching store, always with an undo.

test.control: Default store for everyone on that URL.
test.treatment: Locale offer or route, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Among visitors who met the locale-mismatch rule, compare the switch offer with the unchanged store. Measure successful task starts after switching and track undo, bounce, and manual store changes.
test.primaryMetric: First-session task start after the switch (search, PDP, signup).
test.guardrail: Undo rate and bounce. If people flee the "helpful" store, you guessed wrong.

pitfalls: Hard-redirecting VPN or travel traffic with no undo.
Translating the nav and leaving checkout in the default language.
Treating language as a personalization "win" instead of a prerequisite.

opportunities.title: They came back mid-search and had to start over.
opportunities.summary: Put them back where they left off.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A search, a filtered catalog, a half-read collection, a configured product. They come back and the slate is blank. The polite word is "session". The honest word is "amnesia".
opportunities.whyItEarns: Restoring state can remove substantial repeat work without requiring a sensitive inference. It is personalization as manners.
opportunities.confusion: You do not need to "know" the person. A durable session, a saved search, or a "pick up where you left off" is enough.

signals.example: Prior search, filters, cart, or scroll position on return.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Offer to resume when the visitor returns within 14 days, the prior session contains at least one search plus a filter, saved item, configured product, or meaningful reading position, and the task was not completed. On shared or unrecognized devices, show a resume option rather than restoring automatically.

arms.low: A dismissible "continue last search" chip.
arms.medium: Restore filters and results, with a clear "start fresh".
arms.high: A resume home: last search, last items, last article, last config.

test.treatment: Restored state with an escape hatch.
test.primaryMetric: Resume-to-conversion or task completion.
test.guardrail: People who wanted a new job and felt trapped. Measure "start fresh" use.

pitfalls: Restoring a gift-shopping session onto a later personal visit.
No expiry. A search from March should not haunt September.
Restoring on shared devices without a quiet default.

opportunities.title: They've been reading. You still send them the blog index.
opportunities.summary: Give them the next piece of what they've been reading.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Three whitepapers, two webinars, a pricing glance. Next visit, the resource hub is alphabetical. You could assemble the next useful thing. You show a feed instead.
opportunities.whyItEarns: B2B and media journeys are long. The gift is synthesis: "here's the thread you've been pulling".
opportunities.confusion: A "recommended for you" widget of popular posts is not this. This is a reading path built from their actual path.

signals.example: Content topics, completion depth, recency, and any form fills across visits.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Require at least three substantially consumed pieces on the same topic across two sessions in 30 days, or two pieces plus a related webinar or pricing view. Do not infer a lasting interest from one article.

arms.low: A "continue this topic" row on the next relevant page.
arms.medium: A short path of 3 next pieces plus the matching product or plan.
arms.high: A living brief: what they have seen, what is missing, a human offer if the account is high-value.

test.control: Default resource hub or homepage modules.
test.treatment: Path-aware next-best content.
test.audienceReadout: Among visitors who met the topic-depth rule, compare the assembled path with the standard resource index. Measure progression to the next useful action, not total content views, and report results separately for anonymous and known visitors.
test.primaryMetric: Content-assisted pipeline or subscriber conversion.
test.guardrail: Time-on-site vanity. If they read more and buy less, you built a library, not a path.

pitfalls: Recommending the thing they just finished.
Gating the next piece after they already earned trust.
Sales outreach that recites their reading history back to them.

opportunities.title: The cart is missing the thing that goes with it.
opportunities.summary: Offer that piece, not a random add-on.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A tent without stakes. A camera without a card. A shirt without the usual care kit. Basket analysis plus this cart says something is missing. The page still shows "you may also like" scented candles.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Keep the offer inline, useful, and easy to test. A true complement is not decoration. It helps the customer complete the job already represented by the cart.
opportunities.confusion: Cross-sell is only personalization when it is about the job in the cart, not leftover merchandising slots.

signals.example: Current cart contents and category.
Affinity: customers buying this camera frequently add a compatible SD card before paying.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Show a complement only when its attach rate is at least twice the category baseline in a sufficiently large set of completed orders, it is compatible with the exact cart item, and the customer does not already own or have it in the cart.

arms.low: One well-named complement under the cart line item. Easy to ignore.
arms.medium: Inline add with a reason ("most people add a spare").
arms.high: A "complete the job" bundle, still optional, with a one-click add.

test.treatment: Inline complement based on cart contents.
test.audienceReadout: Among carts eligible for the same complement rule, compare the inline offer with a no-offer holdout. Measure attach rate and order value alongside checkout completion, returns, and removal of the suggested item.
test.primaryMetric: Complement attach rate and average order value, alongside checkout conversion.
test.guardrail: Checkout drop-off. If the module adds friction, kill it.

pitfalls: Three carousels. One complement.
Recommending a second of the same item they already have.
Inserting the module above the checkout button on mobile.

opportunities.title: You already know the size, store, or card, and you still ask.
opportunities.summary: Fill in what you already have. Make it easy to change.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A known shopper has a size, a store, a payment method, an address. PDP, cart, and checkout still start from blank. Every extra field is a chance to leave.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Prefill is personalization that feels like manners. It is easy to hold out, easy to reverse, and it only works if the saved value is right.
opportunities.confusion: Autofill from the browser is not the same as using what you stored on purpose.

signals.example: Last purchased size, saved store, default payment, last address.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Prefill only values confirmed in a successful prior transaction or explicitly saved by an authenticated customer. Verify that the value is still valid and available. Suppress size and store defaults when the session shows gift intent, a different recipient, or a location change.

arms.low: A "use last time" hint they can ignore.
arms.medium: Prefill size and store on PDP and cart, with an obvious edit.
arms.high: Express path: last size in stock, last payment, one tap, and a full checkout still available.

test.treatment: Saved-value defaults for known shoppers.
test.primaryMetric: Checkout completion and time-to-pay.
test.guardrail: Wrong-size returns and payment failures. Bad memory is worse than a blank field.

pitfalls: Prefilling a gift session with the shopper's own size.
No way to see or delete what you stored.
Saving a value they never confirmed.

opportunities.title: Six setup steps before they can actually use it.
opportunities.summary: Cut the steps they don't need. A progress bar isn't shorter.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Connect Slack, invite the team, verify a domain, pick a template, import data, then maybe the job. They already signed up. The stall is the length of the path, not a missing prompt. Intervention would catch a stall. Effort is shortening the path.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Activation personalization that only nags them through the same six steps is not a different experience. A shorter path for their use case, or a skip that still works, is.
opportunities.confusion: A progress bar is not less effort. Removing a required step, or doing it for them, is.

signals.example: Onboarding checklist length, required vs optional steps, time-to-first-value by use case.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Use the shorter path when the customer has declared a supported use case and only one setup step is technically required to reach its first-value event. Defer optional steps, but keep security, compliance, data integrity, and plan-required setup mandatory.

arms.low: Keep the steps. Mark the optional ones optional. Let them skip to the job.
arms.medium: One required step for their use case. The rest later, from inside the job.
arms.high: Do the setup from signals you already have (SSO, import, template) and land them in the job.

test.treatment: Short path for that use case, with a holdout.
test.primaryMetric: Time to first value, and first-value rate.
test.guardrail: Later support tickets for skipped setup that was actually required.

pitfalls: Hiding required setup and surprising them mid-job.
A "personalized" checklist that is the same six items in a different order.
Measuring checklist completion instead of the job.

opportunities.title: You know they'll need it again. You still make them hunt.
opportunities.summary: Remind them when they're actually due.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Same SKU, same cadence. Consumable, refill, replenishment. The site waits for them to remember. A reminder, a one-click reorder, or a subscribe option at the right time could remove that repeat effort.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Replenishment is a clear retention benefit because it saves customers a trip they already take. The timing should come from a reliable pattern, not a guess.
opportunities.confusion: Subscribe-and-save shoved on the first purchase is not this. This is timing the ask to a pattern you have already observed.

signals.example: Repeat SKU purchases with a detectable interval.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Wait for at least three completed purchases of the same replenishable item. Predict a due window only when the intervals are reasonably stable, such as within 20% of the customer's median interval. Suppress the reminder after another purchase, return, or cancellation.

arms.low: A reorder button in account or email near the predicted date. No auto-ship.
arms.medium: A timely reminder with one-click add, plus an optional subscribe.
arms.high: A replenishment plan they opt into, with skip/pause that actually works.

test.treatment: Timed reorder / subscribe offer.
test.audienceReadout: Among customers who met the cadence rule, compare the timed reminder with no cadence-based reminder. Measure incremental repeat purchase and time between orders, then monitor unsubscribes and reminders sent after the need was already resolved.
test.primaryMetric: Repeat purchase rate and time-between-orders.
test.guardrail: Cancellations and "stop emailing me about this".

pitfalls: Predicting a cycle from two purchases.
Charging a subscription they did not mean to start.
Reminding them the week after they already reordered elsewhere.

opportunities.title: You have their history. Next time still starts from scratch.
opportunities.summary: Ask to save one useful default, when it would actually help.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Sizes, brands, notification cadence, favorite store, default replenishment. None of it is saved. Every visit is a fresh interrogation of a person you already know.
opportunities.whyItEarns: A preference the customer confirms is more reliable than a hidden inference. Ask for one useful default after value has been delivered, then use it consistently and visibly.
opportunities.confusion: A 20-field preference center is not a gift. One useful default ("save this size?") at the right moment is.

signals.example: Repeat purchases or usage with empty preference fields.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Ask to save a default after the same value appears in at least two successful purchases or three completed tasks and the corresponding preference field is empty. Prompt only after success, and suppress it after dismissal until another confirming event occurs.

arms.low: A single save prompt after a successful order or session.
arms.medium: Pre-filled defaults they can confirm, not a blank form.
arms.high: A short "make this easier" pass that writes defaults into browse, recs, and messages.

test.treatment: In-moment save / confirm defaults.
test.primaryMetric: Preference save rate, then repeat conversion or time-to-task.
test.guardrail: Form abandonment and opt-outs.

pitfalls: Asking before they have received value.
Using saved prefs to lock them out of discovery.
Never letting them see or delete what you stored.

opportunities.title: A member still gets the generic homepage.
opportunities.summary: Put reorder and their benefits first. The brochure can wait.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Loyalty, subscription, or repeat buyer. Offers, merchandising, and the first screen ignore the membership they already paid for. They have to hunt for reorder, early access, or the thing they always buy.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Serving a known member the stranger experience wastes information that could make the return visit easier. The identity and membership relationship are already established.
opportunities.confusion: A "welcome back, FirstName" bar is not a member experience. Putting their reorder and their tier benefits first is.

signals.example: Loyalty tier, last order, saved items, subscription status.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Show the member home to authenticated customers with an active loyalty tier, paid membership, or current subscription. Confirm that benefits and status are current before rendering them. Delinquent, expired, or disputed memberships receive the standard account path plus a status explanation.

arms.low: Keep the default. A member chip that jumps to reorder and benefits.
arms.medium: Swap the first module: their usual, their tier, a start-fresh.
arms.high: A member home: reorder, benefits, new-for-you. Catalog still one tap away.

test.treatment: Member-first first screen, with a holdout.
test.primaryMetric: Repeat purchase or benefit-use from home.
test.guardrail: New-product discovery. Don't lock them to last year's basket.

pitfalls: Hiding the catalog behind membership modules.
Showing a tier they no longer have.
A first-name greeting with generic merchandising underneath.

opportunities.title: Adding more is harder than the first time they bought.
opportunities.summary: Let them add from the screen they're already on.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Invite a seat, add a line, attach a warranty, lift a cap. Default is a full billing flow, a new cart, or a sales form. They are mid-job. The stall is the work to say yes, not the offer.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Effort at expansion is shortening a path they already want. Prefill, in-flow add, skip the second account. Test against the long checkout they already survived once.
opportunities.confusion: A bigger "Upgrade" button is not less effort. Finishing from the screen they are on is.

signals.example: Account, plan, the add-on they started, billing already on file.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Use the shortened expansion flow when an authorized billing user starts a specific add-on, the account has a valid payment method and accepted terms, and the change is available through self-service. Route price exceptions, contract changes, missing authority, and regulated purchases to the appropriate approval flow.

arms.low: Keep the flow. Prefill who they are and what they already have.
arms.medium: Add from the current screen. Confirm, no second cart.
arms.high: One-tap add for the thing they just hit, receipt in-product, undo for a day.

test.control: Default add-seat, add-on, or second-checkout flow.
test.treatment: Short in-flow add, with a holdout.
test.primaryMetric: Completed expansion of the started add.
test.guardrail: Accidental adds and refunds. One-tap must be reversible.

pitfalls: One-click charges with no undo.
Sending them to a generic pricing page mid-job.
A sales-assisted flow for a $10 add-on.

opportunities.title: They read deeply on the first visit, then start to leave.
opportunities.summary: Offer a relevant next step they can skip, or leave them alone.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A new reader finishes most of a long article, opens another story on the same topic, and then moves to leave. That pattern suggests medium intent, but the reader has not declared a preference. The default response is an email-capture popup unrelated to what they read.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Test a quiet next step against doing nothing. The signal is inferred, so the treatment should remain easy to ignore and should not write a lasting preference without permission.
opportunities.confusion: Inferred interest is not consent. Reading two climate-policy articles does not justify subscribing the reader to a newsletter or declaring that climate is a permanent preference.

signals.example: First session, two substantially completed articles on the same topic, no subscription or follow action, and exit starting.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Count an article as substantially completed after at least 70% scroll depth and 60 seconds of active reading. Trigger only after two qualifying articles in the same topic during the first session. Do not trigger from background tabs or rapid scrolling.

arms.low: Show the next climate-policy article in the normal related-content area.
arms.medium: Offer "Follow climate policy" or "See this week's climate briefing" in a dismissible inline card.
arms.high: If the reader chooses to follow the topic, use that declared preference to shape the next visit and subscription offer.

test.treatment: Topic-relevant next step for qualifying first-session readers, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Among first-session readers who met the two-article rule, compare the topic-relevant treatment with standard related content. Measure topic follows, subscription exploration, and another substantial read without combining them with low-intent first-page visitors.
test.primaryMetric: Topic follow, subscription exploration, or another substantially read article.
test.guardrail: Immediate exits, dismissals, and lower article completion.

pitfalls: An email modal before the reader demonstrates interest.
Treating one article view as medium intent.
Saving an inferred topic as a permanent preference without asking.

opportunities.title: They filtered until there was nothing left.
opportunities.summary: Clear the filter that emptied the grid. Show what comes back.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Facets, price, size, dates. The combination returns zero. Default is a blank grid and "try removing a filter". That is a stall mid-job, not a search-results problem. They were close. Then the path died.
opportunities.whyItEarns: A close match, a "drop this one facet", or a human is a different experience that is easy to hold out. Null filter is as honest a signal as null search.
opportunities.confusion: Zero-results search is a query problem, covered in case 5. A dead filter is a recovery problem. They narrowed successfully, then one more choice removed everything. Help them back one step.

signals.example: Facet combination that returns zero, or a grid that dropped from many to none this session.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger when the latest filter reduces a result set from at least 10 items to zero. Preserve every earlier filter and identify the single filter that caused the dead end. A query that started at zero belongs to search recovery instead.

arms.low: Name the dead facet. One-tap remove. Show how many come back.
arms.medium: Keep the rest of the filters, offer the nearest in-stock or in-range set, with a reason.
arms.high: Recover into a close match plus a way to ask, and remember the combination if they return.

test.treatment: Dead-end recovery, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Among sessions where one filter caused the 10-to-zero drop, compare guided recovery with the standard empty state. Measure recovered detail views and purchases, then inspect whether users immediately restore the removed filter.
test.primaryMetric: Recovered product view or add-to-cart from that session.
test.guardrail: People who wanted zero (true miss) being pushed a mismatch.

pitfalls: Auto-clearing every filter they set.
Showing out-of-budget items as "close".
Counting the recovery click as success when the item is still wrong.

opportunities.title: They left with items in the cart.
opportunities.summary: Remind them of the actual items. Discount last, not first.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: A cart exists and the session ended. The default is a generic reminder the next day, or silence. Neither reflects the likely situation: they already chose, then something interrupted the purchase.
opportunities.whyItEarns: This is intervention, not a newsletter. One reminder of the actual items, a real delivery or stock reason to return, and a holdout. Discounts are a last resort, not the first email.
opportunities.confusion: Three cart emails in three days is not catching them. It is crowding them.

signals.example: Cart contents, time since last checkout step, stock and price at abandon.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Mark a cart abandoned when it contains at least one in-stock item, no matching order was completed, and the checkout has been inactive for at least two hours. Send a reminder only through a permitted channel, suppress it after purchase or cart deletion, and revalidate price and stock before displaying the items.

arms.low: One reminder of the exact items. Then stop.
arms.medium: One reminder plus a reason (stock, delivery window) and an easy dismiss.
arms.high: In-session save on the next visit, plus one message if they do not return.

test.control: No recovery, or the default sequence.
test.treatment: Cart-named recovery with a holdout.
test.primaryMetric: Recovered checkout, not email clicks.
test.guardrail: Unsubscribes and discount dependence.

pitfalls: A coupon on the first touch.
Reminding them of an item that went out of stock.
Firing while they are still in another tab.

opportunities.title: They looked at the same thing a few times and left.
opportunities.summary: A quiet save on the third look, not a popup on the first.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Three PDPs, a pricing page, a doc, then exit. The inference is interest. The failure might be confidence, effort, or a bad page. Intervention means a light, skippable next step, not a takeover.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Test a quiet return path, such as save, compare, or ask, against doing nothing. The signal is uncertain, so the response should remain light and easy to dismiss.
opportunities.confusion: Exit intent is not consent. A third view is only a hypothesis. This case offers a low-pressure return path. "They keep coming back to the same product. They still won't buy." addresses the confidence gap on the page itself.

signals.example: Repeat views of one product or plan, no cart, and no completed decision.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Require at least three views of the same item across two sessions in 14 days, with no cart, trial, or purchase. Offer the save or compare path on the third qualifying view rather than waiting for cursor-exit detection.

arms.low: Nothing in-session. A later note only if they already gave you a channel.
arms.medium: A dismissible "save this" or "compare" on the third view, not on exit.
arms.high: On return, that item first, with proof at the point of commit.

test.treatment: Third-view save or return-path, with a holdout.
test.audienceReadout: Among visitors who met the third-view rule, compare the save or compare option with no intervention. Measure later conversion of that item and track dismissals, saves never reopened, and cross-item purchases.
test.primaryMetric: Later conversion of that item.
test.guardrail: Scroll depth and bounce. If the chip disrupts the page, remove it.

pitfalls: A modal on first product view.
Treating comparison research as abandonment.
Retargeting ads that follow them louder than the site did.

opportunities.title: They paid. Then they never started setup.
opportunities.summary: Give them one first step. Not a tour of everything.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: The receipt went out. Login happened, or didn't. Setup step 1 is untouched. Welcome email #1 is a product tour of everything, which is the opposite of a first step.
opportunities.whyItEarns: One specific first action is more useful than a generic "welcome to the platform" when the account has not started setup.
opportunities.confusion: Onboarding is not a tour. It is getting this person to their first useful outcome.

signals.example: Purchase or signup timestamp with zero setup events.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger when a paid account or qualified signup has recorded no setup event within 24 hours and no teammate or implementation partner is actively completing setup. Exclude refunded, cancelled, fraudulent, and sales-assisted accounts with a scheduled onboarding session.

arms.low: Leave the product alone. One email naming the single first step.
arms.medium: In-product checklist of one to three steps, based on plan or quiz.
arms.high: A guided first-use flow that starts on the job they bought for, with a skip.

test.treatment: First-step-specific empty state and message.
test.primaryMetric: Setup started within 7 days, then first-value event.
test.guardrail: Unsubscribes and repeated attempts to skip the tour.

pitfalls: Five emails before they have opened the product.
A tour that covers features they will not use for months.
No distinction between "hasn't logged in" and "logged in and froze".

opportunities.title: They started setup, then disappeared mid-step.
opportunities.summary: Remind them of the unfinished step. Then stop.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Setup is 40% done. No session in 72 hours. The default is either silence or a drip that recites features. Neither names the unfinished step.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Intervention is not nagging. It is a specific, skippable reminder of the next unfinished step, plus a way to get help.
opportunities.confusion: Day-3, day-5, day-7 emails with the same hero image are not intervention. One note about the actual stuck step is.

signals.example: Last setup step, last seen, and time since.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Treat setup as stalled when progress is greater than 0% but less than 100%, no meaningful setup event has occurred for 72 hours, and the account is still active. Exclude customers who chose "do this later," opened a support case, or have a scheduled onboarding session.

arms.low: One message naming the next step. Then stop.
arms.medium: In-product resume plus one message, with a "do this later" option.
arms.high: Resume flow plus a human assist offer if the account is high-value.

test.treatment: Step-specific resume for stalled setups.
test.primaryMetric: Resume rate and activation within 14 days.
test.guardrail: Unsubscribes and "mark as spam". If you nag, you lose the ones who might have come back.

pitfalls: Restarting the tour from step 1.
Five channels on the same day.
Treating a cancelled customer as stalled.

opportunities.title: The same setup step keeps failing.
opportunities.summary: Give them another way through. Another tooltip won't fix it.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: The same error, the same field, the same OAuth screen, three times. This is not a motivation problem. It is a design or implementation problem showing up as a person.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Personalization here looks like help: a different explanation, a bypass, a human. Measuring it as "engagement" is how you miss churn.
opportunities.confusion: If the same step fails for a cohort, that is a product bug with a name, not a targeting opportunity.

signals.example: Error events, retries, time-on-step, support searches.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger failure-aware help after the same error code occurs three times within 15 minutes or time on the step exceeds twice its normal completion time. Suppress personalized help during a known outage and route the event to incident messaging instead.

arms.low: Inline error copy that names the likely cause and a doc jump.
arms.medium: An alternate path (skip, later, different auth, sample data).
arms.high: A live assist offer after N failures, plus a ticket with the step prefilled.

test.treatment: Failure-aware help after repeated attempts.
test.primaryMetric: Step completion after failure, and activation.
test.guardrail: Support volume. Help should drop tickets, not just relocate them.

pitfalls: A chatbot that restates the error.
Forcing the same path because "the tour must complete".
Not logging the failure into the learning memory.

opportunities.title: The trial is ending. They never really used it.
opportunities.summary: Get them to actually try it before the clock runs out.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Days left on a trial. Key activation event never fired. Default is a "your trial ends soon" feature tour. That is a calendar, not a save.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Intervention here is getting them to first value, or offering a human, before the trial becomes a failed invoice. Easy to hold out against the default drip.
opportunities.confusion: More emails as the date approaches is not the same as naming the unfinished first step.

signals.example: Trial end date, missing activation event, last meaningful session, and account fit.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Qualify when three or fewer trial days remain, the defined activation event has not occurred, and there has been no meaningful session for 48 hours. Exclude accounts already working with support or sales.

arms.low: One note that names the first job, then silence.
arms.medium: In-product first-step plus one message, with skip.
arms.high: Guided first-value or a human handoff for high-fit accounts.
