test.treatment: First-value intervention before expiry.
test.audienceReadout: Among trials that met the at-risk rule, compare the first-value intervention with the standard trial-ending sequence. Measure activation before expiry and paid conversion, then report support load and opt-outs.
test.primaryMetric: Activation event before trial end, then conversion.
test.guardrail: Support load and "stop emailing me". Panic sequences burn the ones who might have converted later.

pitfalls: Counting logins as activation.
Extending the trial instead of fixing first value.
The same sequence for a champion and a tire-kicker.

opportunities.title: They're using it less. The reply is a coupon.
opportunities.summary: Find out what changed. A discount isn't a diagnosis.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Sessions down, key features untouched, seats idle. The inference is churn risk. The honest response is to find out why, not to spray a win-back.
opportunities.whyItEarns: A proportionate, dismissible check-in plus a useful reason to return addresses the possible problem more directly than an automatic discount.
opportunities.confusion: Inferred churn is a hypothesis. Treat it like one: a test, a holdout, a way to be wrong without being loud.

signals.example: Trailing usage and key-event completion relative to the account's own baseline, not relative to the heaviest users.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger when weekly key-event volume falls below 50% of the account's prior eight-week median for two consecutive weeks, with no planned pause, seasonality flag, or known outage. Require a minimum baseline before calculating decline.

arms.low: Silence on the product. One thoughtful check-in, easy to ignore.
arms.medium: A "what's changed?" note with two useful paths (refresh a workflow, pause).
arms.high: A save offer only if they have already said they might leave. Never as the first move.

test.control: No outreach, or the default win-back.
test.treatment: Baseline-aware, proportionate check-in.
test.audienceReadout: Among accounts that met the same decline rule, compare the check-in with no outreach. Measure recovery of the key event and retained revenue, while tracking opt-outs and replies showing the inference was wrong.
test.primaryMetric: Reactivation of the key event, then retained revenue.
test.guardrail: Opt-outs and "this feels like surveillance" replies.

pitfalls: Comparing them with the heaviest users instead of with their own baseline.
Leading with a discount before asking what broke.
No holdout, so you never know if you caused the save.

opportunities.title: They opened cancel.
opportunities.summary: Ask what broke. Let cancel stay one tap.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Cancel, pause, or downgrade was opened. The default is a wall of discounts or a guilt screen. Neither asks what broke, and neither is easy to complete.
opportunities.whyItEarns: Declared churn intent is the cleanest intervention signal you will get. A real pause, a real skip, a real question, and a holdout, beats a 20% offer as the first frame.
opportunities.confusion: Making cancel hard is not personalization. It is a trap.

signals.example: Cancel/pause/downgrade started, and any reason they typed.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Enter the reason-aware flow when an authorized user opens cancellation, pause, or downgrade for an active subscription. Show a tailored alternative only after they select or type a reason. Keep immediate cancellation available throughout and exclude already-cancelled accounts.

arms.low: Let them finish. A single optional "what happened" plus pause.
arms.medium: Reason-aware save: skip a cycle, change plan, or talk to a person. Cancel still one tap.
arms.high: A save offer only after they named the reason, never as the gate.

test.treatment: Reason-aware save with cancel still easy.
test.primaryMetric: Retained revenue and completed cancels (both matter).
test.guardrail: Time-to-cancel and complaint rate. If cancel got slower, you failed.

pitfalls: A six-step "are you sure".
A discount before you know why.
Counting a pause as a save without watching the next 90 days.

opportunities.title: They hit the limit of the plan they're on.
opportunities.summary: Tell them they hit a wall, and how to keep going. Don't throw up a paywall.
opportunities.whatsGoingOn: Seats, messages, SKUs, storage, a feature gate. They hit it mid-job. Default is a paywall modal. The honest read: they were doing the job, then the product said no. Intervention is a path through, not a billboard.
opportunities.whyItEarns: This is expansion with a conscience. They already proved the need. A clear next plan, a temporary lift, or a human, tested against the hard stop, beats a generic upgrade banner.
opportunities.confusion: Blocking the job to force a credit card is not personalization. Naming the limit and a way through is.

signals.example: Plan, usage vs cap, the action that just failed, account value.

opportunities.eligibilityRule: Trigger when a valid action is blocked because usage has reached 100% of a documented plan limit and no upgrade or temporary exception is already pending. Tailor the path to the exact limit hit, and show it only to users who can upgrade or request approval.

arms.low: Name the limit in-line. A link to compare plans. No modal.
arms.medium: A skippable lift (trial of the next tier, extra seats for 7 days) with a reason.
arms.high: In-flow upgrade for the exact ceiling they hit, plus a human for high-fit accounts.

test.treatment: Limit-aware path through, with a holdout.
test.primaryMetric: Expansion conversion of accounts that hit the cap.
test.guardrail: Support tickets and reports of feeling trapped. A hard stop can increase upgrades while still damaging trust and task completion.

pitfalls: A full-screen paywall on the first brush with the limit.
Recommending the most expensive plan by default.
No way to finish the job they were in.

tools.name: Adobe Target
tools.summary: Uses machine learning (a Random Forest model plus a multi-armed bandit) to automatically select the best-performing, marketer-defined experience for each visitor, rebuilding its model roughly every 24 hours.
strengths: Auto-Target rebuilds its model on a ~24-hour cycle using recent visitor behavior, and falls back to the best overall-performing experience when it can't find a winning personalized one
Full Visual Experience Composer support (custom code, multiple audiences, structural page changes), beyond the lighter Automated Personalization mode
Adobe cites a clothing-retailer case with a 29.09% average lift and $1.7M in lift over ten days using ten category-based experiences at 90% traffic allocation
limits: G2 reviewers describe a long learning curve, complexity in advanced test setup, and call the AI capabilities a "black box"
Reviewers report bugginess since the latest UI update and fragmented customer support
Custom, volume-based enterprise pricing with no public entry-level tier — not built for smaller teams
tools.bestFor: Teams already on Adobe who need server-side or at-scale experience selection and can absorb the implementation lift.
questions: Is the audience definition living in Target or in the CDP?
Can we hold out a true default, not a 'personalized everyone'?

source.claim: Auto-Target serves the most tailored experience to each visitor based on the individual customer profile and the behavior of previous visitors with similar profiles, using a Random Forest algorithm plus a multi-armed bandit approach, rebuilding models roughly every 24 hours.

tools.name: Optimizely Personalization
tools.summary: Delivers real-time, audience-targeted experiences inside the same platform as Optimizely's A/B testing and feature-flagging tools, with audiences built from behavioral, CRM, and Optimizely Data Platform signals.
strengths: Personalization campaigns can be A/B tested against each other directly in-platform, not in a separate tool
Audiences combine multiple conditions with AND/OR logic and can pull real-time segments from Optimizely Data Platform
Feature-flag audience targeting overlaps with the personalization audience model, giving product and growth teams one shared targeting layer
limits: Optimizely's own docs cover feature flags and personalization audiences separately — sharing them across the two systems takes deliberate setup, not automatic overlap
No independent source found confirming or denying holdout/control-group gaps for this product; treat that risk as unverified, not confirmed
tools.bestFor: Teams who already run Optimizely tests and want audience variants inside the same system, not a second platform.
questions: Does every personalized campaign have a default holdout?
Who decides when an audience experience is killed?

source.claim: Optimizely Personalization lets you deliver targeted experiences in real time to different visitors based on their behaviors, and lets you create and manage audiences based on data from multiple sources.

tools.name: Webflow Optimize
tools.summary: Runs three experience types on Webflow sites: standard A/B tests, AI-optimized tests that keep shifting traffic to whatever's currently working instead of calling one winner, and manual rules-based personalization for defined audiences.
strengths: AI-optimized mode never permanently "ends" on a winner — it keeps learning and routing each visitor to what's currently working best for them
Manual personalization mode is explicitly rules-based (define an audience, decide what they see), so teams can skip the AI layer for an auditable rule
Native to Webflow's design/publish flow, avoiding a separate tag-manager implementation
limits: Pricing stacks: Optimize A/B testing starts around $299/mo on top of a Webflow site plan, and adding Analyze pushes cost well past a typical Webflow budget
Localize (multilingual) is incompatible with any Ecommerce plan, per third-party review coverage
Not a CDP or product-analytics layer — personalization logic lives only inside Webflow's own session data
tools.bestFor: Marketing sites that need to test and swap experiences without a six-month implementation, and can tolerate Webflow's own pricing tiers.
questions: Can we export what ran, for whom, and why?
What happens when the site leaves Webflow?

source.claim: Webflow's manual personalization mode has no experiment — you identify a specific audience and decide that they must see certain messaging or content — distinct from AI-optimized modes that continuously learn.

tools.name: AB Tasty content personalization
tools.summary: Audience- and intent-based content targeting for anonymous visitors, built on live signals (referral source, device, location, scroll depth) rather than login or cookie data. As of September 2026, AB Tasty and VWO merged their brands under the new parent brand Wingify, with each platform still running independently during the transition.
strengths: Built to personalize anonymous traffic using real-time behavioral signals (referral source, device, browser, location, page behavior, scroll depth, time on page, clicks) rather than identity data

AI-assisted audience creation (Wingz AI, post-merger) surfaces suggested segments with visible signal composition, traffic share, and revenue at stake, so a person approves or overrides rather than trusting a black box
Vendor materials draw an explicit line between A/B testing and personalization, which helps keep a shared backlog honest about what's an experiment vs. a standing rule
limits: Mid-rebrand: product, brand, and likely UI are actively changing as AB Tasty and VWO consolidate under Wingify — confirm what specifically survives the merger before signing
Audience logic can outgrow the UI as campaigns pile up
No G2/TrustRadius cons specific to this product were found in this pass — a research gap, not a clean bill of health
tools.bestFor: CRO-led teams who want content targeting next to A/B tests, with eyes open that the vendor is mid-merger.
questions: Are personalized campaigns in the same backlog as experiments?
Given the Wingify merger, what's the migration path and what stays supported?

source.claim: A/B testing compares different versions of an experience to learn which one performs better. Personalization uses data about visitors, segments, behavior, or intent to deliver different experiences to different audiences — reaching anonymous visitors using real-time signals like referral source, device, browser, location, page behavior, scroll depth, time on page, and clicks.

tools.name: Bloomreach Ecommerce Search
tools.summary: AI-driven ecommerce search and discovery platform (Loomi AI) that personalizes ranking, recommendations, and merchandising from first-party shopper data.
strengths: Continuous behavioral ranking: a Canadian Tire executive is quoted describing Bloomreach as constantly tracking user behavior and readjusting the search results sequence
Loomi AI targets null-result elimination, synonym generation, and autosuggestions, not just top-of-funnel search
Bundles search with merchandising rules and a revenue dashboard, so ranking and boosting live in one admin surface
limits: Discovery, Engagement, and Content are sold and run as three separate products with separate admin interfaces — G2 reviewers describe them as feeling like separate companies under one brand
No public pricing; third-party estimates put Discovery-only at $60K-$120K/yr, with 3-9 month reported implementation timelines
Revenue-lift language ("20% or more") is vendor-reported, not independently audited
tools.bestFor: Retailers with enough engineering and merchandising headcount to run a dedicated search stack, not teams wanting a lightweight bolt-on.
questions: Are we buying Discovery alone, or paying for Engagement/Content modules we won't use?
Do we have a ranking holdout to separate Loomi's lift from normal seasonality?

source.claim: Loomi AI captures every search, purchase, click, return, preference, and detail on each shopper, and continuously readjusts search result sequencing based on behavior.

tools.name: Customer.io
tools.summary: Event-triggered lifecycle messaging across email, push, SMS, and in-app, built on a customer profile and behavior-data layer.
strengths: Automations trigger on segment, event, form, relationship, date, or webhook — genuine event-based triggering, not just list sends
Full API/webhook access plus a built-in CDP-style profile layer
Rated 4.4/5 across 846 G2 reviews, with reviewers citing real-time event-driven automation as a top strength
limits: Steep learning curve for advanced automation logic, per G2 cons
Per-profile pricing counts all contacts, including dormant/deleted ones — a recurring billing complaint in reviews
tools.bestFor: Product-led SaaS and ecommerce teams who want messages triggered by actual in-product behavior, not calendar sends.
questions: Does every campaign check product state at send time?
What is the maximum number of touches in 7 days?

source.claim: You can build automations using customer profiles, events, account relationships, and other real-time data — every workflow can respond to what customers are doing now.

tools.name: Twilio Segment Unify
tools.summary: Builds unified, real-time customer profiles from event and identity data (Unify), which other tools consume for activation.
strengths: Deterministic identity resolution using a rules-based Identity Graph matches userId, anonymousId, email, and custom external IDs into one profile per person
Profile API lets teams query traits, events, and identifiers programmatically to feed personalization or engagement tools
Handles anonymous-to-known stitching across web, mobile, server, and third-party touchpoints
limits: Unify requires Segment's Business tier — identity resolution isn't available on lower plans
G2 reviewers report hypersegmentation is complicated or not possible, and note the absence of built-in ML pipelines for advanced audience logic
It's plumbing, not delivery — Segment hands profiles to whatever tool runs the actual experience
tools.bestFor: Teams who keep losing 'who is this person' across web, app, and email and need one profile before they can pick a delivery tool.
questions: Which events are actually used in a live experience?
Who owns identity resolution when two tools disagree?

source.claim: Segment first searches the Identity Graph for incoming external IDs; if it finds multiple matching profiles, it applies the identity resolution settings to add the event to the appropriate profile.

tools.name: Salesforce Personalization
tools.summary: AI-driven, real-time decisioning engine built on Salesforce Data 360 that updates customer profiles on every interaction and recommends next-best content or offers across web, email, mobile, and Agentforce conversations.
strengths: Profiles update in real time on every click, view, or purchase, feeding an AI decisioning engine that determines what content or recommendation to serve, where, when, and how
Integrates directly with Agentforce via a "Get User Intent" action, so live agent-conversation signals feed the same decisioning engine as web/email personalization
Extends decisioning across sales, service, commerce, and loyalty using the same underlying data, per Salesforce's own claim
limits: G2 reviews of the related Marketing Cloud Personalization product describe complex setup, a steep learning curve, and functions that need SQL to get full value
Reviewers note the product is organized into separate 'studios' with inconsistent UI between them, and report sessions hanging and requiring re-login
Depends on Salesforce Data 360 and CRM data quality — the engine is only as good as the underlying account/profile data
tools.bestFor: B2B teams whose best signal is already in Salesforce and who have technical resources to run a studio-based, SQL-adjacent platform.
questions: What does the page do when the account match is wrong?
Is marketing allowed to change an experience without a Salesforce ticket?

source.claim: The engine learns from every click and lets that insight shape the next piece of content or offer a visitor is served, analyzing browsing behavior and intent signals to predict which offer will motivate each individual in that specific moment.

tools.name: Appcues
tools.summary: In-product engagement platform for building targeted flows, tooltips, checklists, and announcements without engineering.
strengths: Flow Builder covers tooltips, hotspots, modals, and checklists, with audience targeting/segmentation built in
Launchpads give users a persistent, app-embedded menu to flows and resources, not just a one-shot tour
Cross-channel workflows can trigger in-app content, email, or push off behavior or inactivity, not just in-app alone
limits: Even on the Grow plan (~$50K MAU tier), Appcues caps published experiences at 25 — a real ceiling once checklists, announcements, surveys, and tours are each counted separately
G2 reviewers cite a dated/clunky UI, "spotty" flow behavior, and slow flow transitions
Reporting and analytics are called out by reviewers as limited relative to expectations
tools.bestFor: Product teams who need first-step and resume experiences shipped fast, without an engineering queue.
questions: Can the user dismiss this forever?
Does it fire on the failing step, or on every login?

source.claim: Even on the Grow plan ($50K MAUs), Appcues caps you at 25 published experiences.

tools.name: Pendo in-app guides
tools.summary: Product experience platform combining usage analytics with in-app guides targeted by user or account segments.
strengths: Segmentation is powered by analytics and metadata, letting teams target guides at the user or account level, not just broad cohorts
Analytics and guides live in one system (Data Explorer, funnels, retention, Product Engagement Score) so targeting can be built off actual usage data
Guide types range from lightboxes and banners to tooltips, checklists, and a resource center, not one tour format
limits: Behavioral data processes in batches with roughly an hour of latency before it shows in dashboards or can trigger a guide — not real-time for teams that need to intervene the moment friction hits
Custom guide styling frequently requires CSS/engineering involvement despite the "no-code" positioning, per reviewers
Pricing is opaque (all tiers say "Request pricing"), and reviewers call the licensing model inflexible, with enterprise contracts reported north of $130K/year
tools.bestFor: Product-led teams who will treat guides as experiments with owners, not a permanent layer of one-off pop-ups.
questions: Given the ~1-hour data latency, which guides genuinely need real-time triggering, and which are fine on a delay?
Who owns pruning stale guides, and what's the kill criterion before we ship a new one?

source.claim: Segmentation in Pendo, powered by analytics and metadata, allows you to target guides at the user or account level.

tools.name: Monetate
tools.summary: Retail-focused "Experience Optimization Platform" combining AI-driven personalization/recommendations, merchandising, and no-code/server-side A/B testing under one engine (MONET), backed by a managed-services "Concierge" team.
strengths: Combines no-code, zero-flicker experimentation with server-side experimentation in the same suite, avoiding a separate CRO tool
Retail-native positioning: merchandising, testing, and 1:1 personalization framed as one workflow, not three products
Concierge managed-services team is a real differentiator for retailers who don't want to own day-to-day optimization work
limits: G2 reviewers say the UI "doesn't look as advanced as the tool is" and want more flexible data analytics, including custom statistical-significance thresholds instead of Monetate's defaults
Reviewers want real-time reporting — some report waiting weeks for results after launching a test
G2 comparison coverage notes competitors consistently outperform Monetate on ease of administration, support quality, and setup ease
tools.bestFor: Retailers who want onsite testing, merchandising, and targeting in one retail-native suite and can accept a less modern UI in exchange for managed-services support.
questions: Is there a true control for 1:1?
Who merchandises the personalized slots?

source.claim: Monetate describes itself as an Experience Optimization Platform combining AI, personalization, recommendations, and experimentation in a single, unified solution, with server-side and no-code, zero-flicker, enterprise-grade experimentation.

tools.name: Demandbase Personalization
tools.summary: ABM platform module that identifies visiting accounts via AccountID (firmographic, intent, technographic signals) and swaps page copy, images, CTAs, and links for those accounts, plus auto-fills company data on forms.
strengths: AccountID uses NLP-based content validation intended to reduce false-positive account identification, per the vendor's own methodology
Site Customization can target both account-level and people-segment criteria, including intent signals
Auto-fills firmographic form fields to reduce visitor friction while still capturing B2B attributes
limits: Neither the product page nor the vendor's own blog on this topic describes a fallback or 'not your company?' experience for misidentified visitors — confirm that exists rather than assume it
Vendor's own guidance warns that a high match rate with lower accuracy is useless, and recommends starting with four to five key segments at a time, implying a real accuracy/scale tradeoff
G2 reviews of the broader Demandbase One platform cite onboarding length, contract rigidity, and UI complexity
tools.bestFor: ABM programs that will always show a 'not your company?' escape and start with a small number of target segments rather than a broad rollout.
questions: What is the false-positive rate on account ID?
Do we hold out a set of target accounts?

source.claim: A high match rate with lower accuracy is useless if you want to personalize website experiences; keeping web personalization simple often gives the best outcomes, focusing on four to five key segments at a time.

tools.name: Kameleoon Audiences
tools.summary: Experimentation platform with an AI Predictive Targeting feature that scores each visitor's likelihood to convert (0-100) and lets you target or exclude by that score.
strengths: Propensity scoring runs via a single script, with no separate data project required
Falls back to your other targeting conditions while the model is still learning, so a segment doesn't break during ramp-up
Predefined likelihood bands (Very low to Very high) or a custom 0-100 range for finer control
limits: The model needs 7 days and 100,000 visits by default before it activates — not viable for lower-traffic sites or short campaigns
Docs don't describe a formal on/off toggle for the AI condition mid-test; it just falls back to other conditions rather than offering a clean disable
G2 reviewers note a real learning curve, and that complex tests often need developer help
tools.bestFor: Teams who want one vendor for tests and audience experiences and already clear 100k+ monthly visits.
questions: Can we turn predictive off and still run the test, or does it just silently fall back to other conditions?
Do we have the traffic (100k+ visits/7 days) to make the propensity score meaningful, or will it stay in learning mode?

source.claim: The AI model needs 7 days and 100,000 visits by default before it becomes operational; during the learning phase the likelihood-to-convert condition stays inactive and the segment relies on other active conditions.

tools.name: Dynamic Yield
tools.summary: Personalization and recommendations platform with a merchandising engine and Experience APIs for running recs and server-side experiments on any channel.
strengths: Multiple recommendation algorithms (deep learning, viewed-together, bought-together, popularity, recently viewed), not just one model
Merchandising rules connect to CRM/segmentation data, so recs can be pinned or filtered rather than left purely algorithmic
Experience APIs support server-side deployment on any device, not just an onsite widget
limits: Starting price around $35,000/year per pricing research — out of reach for smaller catalogs or teams running only a few campaigns
G2 reviewers cite developer dependence and time-consuming integrations, especially for custom HTML/CSS/JS work
Some reviewers note limited built-in analytics relative to dedicated BI tools
tools.bestFor: Commerce teams whose personalization is mostly recs and merchandising and who have enterprise budget and dev support.
questions: Where is the recs holdout, and can we see lift numbers separate from merchandising rule overrides?
How much custom dev work will implementation actually take beyond the packaged widgets?

source.claim: Dynamic Yield's merchandising engine creates recommendation rules that automatically update widgets according to context, behavior, and historical data, using algorithms including deep learning, viewed together, popularity, recently viewed, and bought together.

tools.name: VWO Testing
tools.summary: Testing platform with audience/behavior targeting and a visual editor; personalization runs as a separate module from Experimentation. As of September 2026, VWO and AB Tasty merged their brands under the new parent brand Wingify, with each platform still running independently during the transition.
strengths: Visual editor lets marketers change copy, CTAs, images, and forms without code
Targeting combines device, browser, location, traffic source, and on-site behavior (clicks, scroll, exit intent) with filter logic
Live preview lets you verify a variation renders correctly for a targeted audience before launch
limits: Personalization runs as a distinct product suite from Experimentation — no evidence personalized variants live inside the same A/B test object
G2 reviewers flag a steep learning curve for non-technical users and a buggy/clunky UI in places
Reviewers note extra fees for features like separate device reporting, and limits on inserting new content blocks via the visual editor
tools.bestFor: Teams starting to test audience variants without a new CDP, especially marketers who want to move without engineering tickets.
questions: Is the personalized variant actually in the same experimentation backlog and reporting, or does it live in a separate module with separate data?
Who QAs flicker and layout shift from visual-editor edits against our design system?

source.claim: Update copy, CTAs, images, forms, banners, and more with a point-and-click editor — no code needed — and target experiments by audience, context, and behavior, so each test reaches the visitors it was built for.

tools.name: Iterable
tools.summary: Cross-channel journeys (email, SMS, push, in-app) built from a single visual studio, triggered by real-time customer behavior.
strengths: Real-time, adaptive logic moves past static if/then rules — journeys adapt to the individual in milliseconds, per the vendor
Single studio spans email, SMS, push, and in-app so channel coordination isn't a separate build
Nova Intelligence / Channel Optimization uses historical data to pick the highest-performing channel per user
limits: No public pricing — every deal starts with sales, and enterprise contracts run from roughly $20K/year into the hundreds of thousands, with a steep learning curve requiring engineering/data resources
Journey complexity plus the lack of a self-serve trial means procurement and setup overhead is real, not just a feature gap
tools.bestFor: Lifecycle teams with engineering support who will put every journey through a holdout and kill rule, not marketers wanting a quick self-serve start.
questions: What is the holdout for this journey?
What is the maximum concurrent journeys per person?

source.claim: Real-time, adaptive logic builds seamless paths across email, SMS, push, and in-app from a single studio.

tools.name: Braze
tools.summary: Cross-channel messaging platform (push, email, SMS, in-app, WhatsApp, and more) that orchestrates sends off real-time customer behavior.
strengths: Consolidates 8 channels (email, mobile push, web push, SMS/RCS, WhatsApp, LINE, KakaoTalk, digital ads via Audience Sync) into one orchestration layer
Frequency capping works across the whole customer, not per-channel — caps can apply to email, push, SMS, and webhooks together
Behavior-triggered orchestration: real-time customer behaviors and cross-channel interactions can dictate the next message
limits: In-app messages and Content Cards are explicitly excluded from frequency capping per Braze's own docs — the two most product-native channels are the ones you can least throttle
Caps reset on calendar days, not rolling 24-hour windows, so a user can get capped messages at 11pm and again an hour later
At high volume (100+ messages/channel), frequency capping by tag may not enforce reliably — Braze recommends a weekly volume cap as a backstop
tools.bestFor: App-led products that can fire messages off real product-usage events, not just marketing list membership.
questions: Since in-app and Content Cards sit outside frequency caps, how do we prevent stacking those with capped channels for the same user?
Are our events clean and real-time enough to trigger next-best-action messaging, or are we really just doing batch segmentation with a Braze wrapper?

source.claim: In-app messages and Content Cards are not counted as or toward caps on campaigns or Canvas components of any type.

tools.name: Algolia
tools.summary: Hosted search infrastructure with rule-based merchandising and an opt-in machine-learning personalization layer.
strengths: Personalization runs as an explicit affinity-scoring layer (clicks, views, purchases) on top of ranking rather than replacing it, so textual relevance and custom ranking stay intact
Rules apply after personalization, giving merchandisers a final override point
A dashboard simulator lets teams preview a personalization strategy's effect on real user profiles before shipping it
limits: Pricing is dual-metric (search requests + indexed records) with AI features gated to premium tiers; reviewers call this the platform's biggest weakness as record counts grow
The product page doesn't document whether personalization can be cleanly A/B tested against a no-personalization baseline — confirm in implementation, don't assume
Record size and per-index attribute limits have forced at least one reported case to split data models
tools.bestFor: Teams with developer resources to tune ranking rules and personalization weights themselves, not those wanting a fully managed black-box engine.
questions: Can we run a clean ranking-with-vs-without-personalization holdout, or does Algolia's architecture make that hard to isolate?
What does our actual record count and query volume put us at on the pricing tiers, including reported 1.5-2x overage rates?

source.claim: Personalization adapts search results based on each user's behavior, preferences, and past interactions; if you use Rules, the engine applies them after Personalization.

tools.name: Mutiny
tools.summary: B2B website personalization tool that identifies visiting companies (via IP/firmographic match) and swaps page content — headlines, proof, CTAs — by account, segment, or industry. As of April 2026 it relaunched as an AI GTM agent, expanding beyond the original website-personalization product.
strengths: Pre-built firmographic data integrations identify visitors by industry, company size, funnel stage, and ad campaign without custom ID work
Account-based personalization can target named high-priority accounts specifically, not just segment buckets
No enterprise CDP required to get account/segment swaps running
limits: G2 reviewers call cross-test analytics the weakest area — no rolled-up reporting across dozens of live personalized pages
CRM integrations (Salesforce, HubSpot) are Enterprise-tier only, starting around $30,000/year; Business-tier teams can't pull CRM data into personalization

The product substantially relaunched in April 2026 (the legacy personalization product was discontinued in its original form) — no independently verified reviews yet exist for the new GTM-agent version
tools.bestFor: B2B marketing sites that need proof and CTA to match the visitor and have real traffic volume to reach significance, not early-stage low-traffic sites.
questions: What's the escape hatch when we guess the account wrong, and is that still true post-relaunch?
Given the April 2026 product relaunch, which parts of any review are about the current product versus the discontinued legacy one?

source.claim: Salesforce and HubSpot integrations are Enterprise-only, starting at $30,000/year, and Business-plan teams can't pull CRM data into asset personalization; Mutiny relaunched on April 8, 2026 as an AI GTM agent, having discontinued its original website-personalization SaaS product.

tools.name: Heap
tools.summary: Autocapture-based product analytics that records clicks, views, form fills, and paths without upfront event instrumentation.
strengths: True autocapture: one snippet records every view, click, swipe, and form fill on web, plus taps/screen views/text inputs on mobile, without a tracking plan
Events can be defined retroactively from already-captured raw data, so a new question doesn't require waiting on new instrumentation
Supplementable with manual/API-based event tracking when autocapture alone isn't specific enough
limits: You store everything autocapture collects whether you need it or not — G2 reviewers cite this as a real cost driver and a signal-to-noise problem
Reviewers describe a steep learning curve and functionality gaps versus dedicated analytics tools, including limited attribution and less-developed mobile app support
Insight is not delivery — autocapture tells you where a different experience might matter, it doesn't build or trigger one
tools.bestFor: Teams who need to find where a different experience would even matter before committing engineering time to instrument it.
questions: Which Heap-sourced insights have actually become tests or shipped experiences, versus staying in a dashboard?
Given the data-storage cost complaints in reviews, do we have a retention/pruning policy, or are we paying to store everything by default?

source.claim: With a single snippet of code, Heap automatically captures every view, click, swipe, and form fill.

tools.name: Sitecore Personalize
tools.summary: Real-time web personalization and A/B/n testing inside Sitecore, driven by live behavioral and contextual signals.
strengths: Ships built-in conditions for affinity, geolocation, device, and behavior, plus custom reusable conditions
Runs A/B/n and multivariate tests on any page variant or content block, promotable in one click across connected sites
Distinguishes anonymous ('visitor') from identified ('customer') guests via real-time identity resolution, upgrading a guest mid-session when matching data arrives
limits: Public docs don't explicitly document holdout/control-group mechanics — confirm directly with Sitecore before assuming a true default group is native
Heavy platform if the only need is a single landing-page swap; it's built as a full decisioning + testing layer
tools.bestFor: Sitecore teams who want experience selection and tests in one place, with identity resolution already tied into the same guest record.
questions: Can we hold out a true default, not personalized-everyone — and where exactly is that configured?
Does the decision run at the component, or only as a popup?

source.claim: Real-time personalization adapts instantly to audience signals with out-of-the-box conditions for affinity, geolocation, device, and behavior; run A/B/n and multivariate experiments and roll out winners in a single click.

tools.name: Nosto
tools.summary: AI commerce platform combining personalized search, recommendations, merchandising, and content/A-B testing under one data layer.
strengths: Search, category merchandising, and recommendations run off the same shopper-affinity data, so results, banners, and content stay consistent
Built-in A/B testing (part of Conversion Optimization) means lift can in principle be measured, not just asserted
A named central AI agent ("Huginn") plus sub-agents run continuously to surface opportunities — a specific product mechanism, not generic AI marketing
limits: G2 reviewers flag significant price increases over time and describe pricing as opaque: custom quotes, sales-gated access, and commission-style billing
Analytics depth is a recurring reviewer complaint
A recs/merchandising engine without an active holdout still can't be priced for lift — the built-in A/B tooling only helps if it's actually configured that way
tools.bestFor: Retailers who want search, recs, and content personalization managed as one connected system rather than stitched from point tools.
questions: Is our contract commission-based, and if so how does that change as personalized AOV grows?
Where specifically is the recs/ranking holdout configured, and is it always-on or something we have to build ourselves?

source.claim: AI-powered ecommerce personalization, search, and merchandising — content, banners, and merchandising adapt to each individual's affinities, from site to app to email.

tools.name: Coveo
tools.summary: Enterprise AI search platform using deep-learning 'product affinities' to personalize ranking, suggestions, and recommendations in real time.
strengths: Uses vector representations of products plus session clickstream to do real-time intent detection, not just historical segment matching
Explicitly targets long-tail visibility, using vectors to ensure visibility beyond the top 20-30% of items — a specific mechanism against the popularity-bias problem most recs engines have
Coveo's own testing claims an additional 4 to 5 percent lift on revenue per visit from the personalization layer (vendor-reported, not third-party audited)
limits: Case-study numbers (Caleres 25% search conversion increase, FleetPride 400% sales growth) are vendor-published and customer-specific — don't assume they transfer
Enterprise-grade platform: implementation and catalog/content quality still gate what the model can actually surface
Product pages don't document a native way to force a non-personalized control group, making in-house lift verification harder
tools.bestFor: Enterprise teams (commerce or B2B/content-heavy sites) that already have clean product and content catalogs and want one AI layer across both.
questions: Can we replicate a version of their reported 4-5% RPV lift with our own holdout, or is that figure not reproducible in our environment?
How much of the 'long tail visibility' claim actually changes our category mix versus just re-ordering the same top sellers?

source.claim: Personalization that inspires purchase and loyalty; product ranking personalizes in real-time based on their most recent site interactions.

tools.name: Constructor
tools.summary: Ecommerce search and recommendations platform that optimizes recs against a chosen business KPI using clickstream data and merchant rules.
strengths: Recs are tied to an explicit, selectable optimization target — RPV, conversion, average order value, or retention — rather than a generic relevance score
Nine distinct recommendation logic sets, with merchandiser-controlled 'searchandizing rules' per pod, so a human can override the model per placement
G2 reviewers score Product Recommendations at 9.8-10.0 and note support for detail-level personalization (e.g., tailoring by stated preferences like inseam or location)
limits: G2 reviewers note recommendations were 'initially very poor' out of the box and needed added business rules to work as intended — real setup overhead, not plug-and-play
KPI-optimized recs need enough traffic and event volume to train against; low-traffic catalogs won't see the reinforcement-learning benefit quickly
Uses reinforcement learning to continuously test and improve, which means the model is always shifting — a holdout has to be maintained deliberately or the baseline drifts
tools.bestFor: Commerce teams with real traffic and a merchandising function willing to actively tune rules pod-by-pod, not a set-and-forget team.
questions: Which KPI is currently set as the optimization target, and who chose it?
What manual rule work did we have to add post-launch to get recommendations to an acceptable baseline?

source.claim: Drive upsells and increase RPV with hyper-personalized product recommendations, optimized toward the outcomes you track — such as RPV, conversion, average order value, or retention.

tools.name: Klaviyo
tools.summary: Behavior-triggered email and SMS with real-time customer profiles and segments, built for ecommerce.
strengths: Builds a complete, 360-degree profile for each customer that updates in real time with every email open, website browse, purchase
Segments update dynamically as customers meet or fall out of conditions
4.6/5 on G2, with reviewers specifically praising the two-way, near-real-time Shopify integration
limits: Pricing scales fast with active profile count; reviewers describe costs as unreasonable at scale, with no annual discount as of 2026
A 90-day suppression cooldown means a suppressed profile stays billable for three months before it can be re-suppressed
tools.bestFor: Ecommerce teams whose best next action is a message, not a homepage rewrite.
questions: Does every flow check product state at send time?
How does the 90-day suppression cooldown affect what we're actually billed for?

source.claim: Klaviyo builds a complete, 360-degree profile for each customer that updates in real time with every email open, website browse, purchase, support ticket, and more.

tools.name: Insider One
tools.summary: Cross-channel engagement platform (web, app, messaging) that builds a unified profile from attributes, real-time behavior, and precomputed predictive scores to drive personalization and campaign targeting.
strengths: 120+ behavioral and predictive attributes computed as part of the unified customer profile (discount affinity, product interest, etc.)
Precomputed scores (purchase likelihood, churn risk, predicted LTV) available instantly rather than needing a live model call
Send Time Optimization and Next Best Channel select timing/channel per user automatically
limits: G2 reviews describe initial implementation as notoriously heavy, dependent on clean internal data and APIs — messy source data makes rollout harder
Some reviewers cite inability to activate certain channels due to incomplete integrations
The predictive layer is still a probabilistic model, not a guarantee — same caveat as other vendors' propensity scoring
tools.bestFor: Teams who need one vendor for onsite, app, and triggered campaigns and can commit to clean underlying data infrastructure.
questions: Can we turn predictive off and still run a clean test against a control group?
What is the actual holdout/measurement approach across web and messaging when they fire together?

source.claim: Use attributes, real-time behavior, and Predictive AI to craft the perfect experience every time.

tools.name: Userpilot
tools.summary: In-app flows, checklists, and multi-channel workflows targeted by behavior and segment, built without code.
strengths: No-code canvas builds multi-step journeys mixing in-app content (modals, tooltips, checklists, surveys) and email in one flow, with conditional branching on behavior, user properties, or segment membership
Triggers fire on real-time product events or time delays, not just page load or login
G2 reviewers rate behavior-responsive messaging highly and single out flexible personalization as a consistent strength
limits: G2 reviewers report segmentation/targeting rules can be confusing and hard to manage as they multiply
Vendor marketing pages are heavy on outcomes and light on documenting targeting mechanics — the specifics live in product/docs pages, not the pitch
tools.bestFor: Product teams who need first-step and resume experiences triggered by real product behavior, without an engineering queue.
questions: Can the user dismiss this forever?
Does it fire on the failing step, or on every login?

source.claim: No-code canvas for multi-step journeys mixing in-app content and email, with conditional branching on behavior, properties, NPS, segment membership, and page visits.

tools.name: Tealium AudienceStream
tools.summary: Server-side CDP that stitches identities in real time and pushes live audiences into 1,300+ connected delivery tools.
strengths: Patented visitor stitching technology builds unified profiles across devices/channels, updating in real time as events arrive
Over 1,300 integrations for activating audiences without custom pipes to each destination
Optional Tealium Predict ML layer scores likelihood of an action (e.g., churn, conversion) to define audiences — a paid add-on, not core AudienceStream
limits: A CDP is not a personalization program — an audience is a segment definition, not a rendered experience; something downstream has to act on it
Predict (the ML/scoring capability) is a premium add-on, so out-of-the-box AudienceStream is rules-based segmentation, not predictive
Profiles and audiences without an activation path just accumulate
tools.bestFor: Teams who keep losing 'who is this person' across channels and need one real-time profile before other tools can act on it.
questions: Which audiences are live in a real experience today, versus defined but never activated?
Are we paying for Predict, or are 'audiences' here just rules-based segments?

source.claim: Create a unified view of your customers across channels, segment your audiences to power personalized experiences, and orchestrate that data to fuel actions.

tools.name: Conductrics
tools.summary: Rule-based and algorithmic (contextual bandit) targeting that reacts to in-session behavior, not just page loads.
strengths: Combines explicit rule-based targeting with contextual multi-armed bandits using Thompson Sampling to shift traffic toward better-performing variants in real time
Triggers fire on specific interactions — cart-open, element scroll-into-view — rather than only on page load
Decisions are exposed as human-readable decision trees, and the platform is SOC 2 Type 2, GDPR, and HIPAA compliant
limits: No G2 reviews or public pricing found — custom quote only, making it hard to benchmark cost or read independent user feedback
A bandit optimizing traffic allocation can quietly erode a true fixed holdout if teams don't explicitly configure one
tools.bestFor: Teams who want on-site experience selection they can explain and audit, not a black-box recs carousel.
questions: Can we keep a true default while the bandit runs, or does it always reallocate toward the leader?
Does the decision fire in the page, or only as a popup?

source.claim: Conductrics triggers personalization based on specific user interactions — such as opening a cart or scrolling a specific element into view — rather than on page loads alone, and uses contextual Multi-Armed Bandits with Thompson Sampling to dynamically allocate traffic toward best-performing variations.

tools.name: Convert Experiences
tools.summary: Website A/B tests and 1:1/segment personalizations built on the same testing infrastructure, with a visual editor and dev-level code hooks.
strengths: Personalization sits in the same platform and workspace as A/B, split-URL, multivariate, and multi-page tests, not a separate tool
Five code levels (global/variation CSS and JS, plus project-wide JS) give developers granular control beyond the WYSIWYG editor
4.7/5 on G2 across 64 reviews, with users citing responsive support and quick CRO execution
limits: Entry 'Starter' plan caps at 5,000 events/month and one workspace — real personalization volume needs a paid tier
G2 reviewers flag tracking and goal-tracking limitations, plus friction in object arrangement
tools.bestFor: CRO teams who will treat a personalized variant as an experiment with a holdout, not a permanent unmeasured swap.
questions: Is every personalization in the same backlog as the tests, or does it bypass QA?
What happens when the audience-matching condition (cookie, UTM, tag) is wrong or stale?

source.claim: 1:1 personalization matches visitor segments to relevant, unique site experiences, targeted via JavaScript conditions, cookies, UTM parameters, page types and custom tags, on the same platform as A/B and multivariate testing.

tools.name: Uniform
tools.summary: Edge-delivered, component-level personalization and testing for composable front ends.
strengths: Personalization decisions resolve at the CDN edge in under 50ms, on Akamai, Cloudflare, Vercel, or Netlify, avoiding third-party script flicker
Targets individual components (e.g., a hero) rather than forking the whole page, so unrelated page elements stay static

Works from first visit using contextual signals (location, device, UTM, time of day) before any behavioral profile exists, with A/B testing on the same infrastructure and per-component uplift/significance reporting
limits: Requires a composable front end (React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, Astro, Angular) — a traditional monolithic CMS site won't get the edge benefit
Public review coverage is thin: no substantial G2 review base as of a September 2026 check, so most proof points are vendor case studies (Telus, VyStar) rather than independent reviews
tools.bestFor: Headless/composable sites that want on-site personalization without a third-party flicker or origin round-trip.
questions: Can we hold out a true default at the component level, not just at the page?
Who owns a signal or resolves the conflict when two experiences both match the same visitor?

source.claim: Uniform personalizes and tests any experience at the edge on any CDN: decisions resolve in under 50ms with no flicker and no third-party script tax; targeting works from first visit using location, device, campaign, and time-of-day signals.

tools.name: Acquia Personalization
tools.summary: No-code website campaigns (A/B, targeted personalization, and content recommendations) built and optimized for Drupal, with a separately documented path for non-Drupal sites.
strengths: Three distinct campaign types — A/B/targeted personalization, content recommendations, and mixed campaigns — each with its own rule-building flow
No-code interface: marketers configure targeting rules without writing code
Acquia documents running Personalization on non-Drupal websites, so it isn't strictly locked to Drupal even though it's optimized for it
limits: Built and optimized for Drupal first; other stacks are a documented but secondary path, likely meaning fewer defaults and more setup

Docs pages for this product returned intermittent server errors during this research, which limited deeper verification of specific rule mechanics — confirm current behavior directly before publishing detailed claims
tools.bestFor: Drupal teams who need on-site content targeting and recommendations in the CMS they already run.
questions: Is there a true default for people who miss every segment?
Can we kill a campaign without a Drupal deploy?

source.claim: Unify data and content to deliver personalized experiences across multiple channels — built and optimized for Drupal.

tools.name: LimeSpot
tools.summary: On-site recommendations plus adaptive headlines, banners, and collections for Shopify, BigCommerce, and SHOPLINE stores.
strengths: Adapts headlines, banners, CTAs, or any HTML section based on customer preferences and behavior, not just a recs widget
Can 'shapeshift' collections per audience segment to pin certain products and sort differently
4.6 stars across 507 reviews on the Shopify App Store — an independent signal of real merchant usage
limits: Marketing and much of the product is scoped to Shopify, BigCommerce, and SHOPLINE — not a universal platform
No active G2 profile found as of this research, so third-party validation outside the Shopify App Store is thin
tools.bestFor: Commerce teams on Shopify/BigCommerce whose personalization is the page in front of the shopper, not the email after they leave.
questions: Where is the holdout for a shapeshifted collection?
Can merchandising pin or suppress when stock says so?

source.claim: Automatically adapt headlines, banners, CTAs, or any HTML section based on customer preferences and behavior.

tools.name: Rebuy
tools.summary: Shopify-native merchandising widgets and bundles across every storefront page, cart through post-purchase.
strengths: Uses Shopify's theme app extension framework, so widgets install without touching theme code
Widgets span homepage to the thank-you page, plus emails, blog posts, and landing pages
Built specifically for growing Shopify and Shopify Plus stores doing $1M+/year, per independent reviews
limits: Shopify-only — not a fit for any other platform
Pricing scales with revenue: Enterprise runs $999/month for up to $40K in Rebuy-generated revenue, then $249 per additional $10K — a real cost gate at scale
tools.bestFor: Shopify Plus teams who will merchandize complements in the path, not after the click-away.
questions: Which page actually gets the widget — home, PDP, or cart?
Can we pin a complement by cart contents, not just affinity?

source.claim: Rebuy merchandising widgets are AI-powered, customizable product displays built to increase AOV and conversion across every page of your Shopify store.

tools.name: Algonomy
tools.summary: Retail personalization suite (search, recs, dynamic listing pages, content/styling, social proof, shopping agent) built on the earlier RichRelevance/Manthan merger — now operating under the ADA brand after ADA acquired Algonomy in July 2026.
strengths: Search, recs, dynamic product listing pages, and content/styling ("ensembles") in one commerce layer, not just a recs pod
Used by 400+ brands, giving it real production scale versus a point solution
limits: The vendor no longer exists as a standalone brand: since the July 2026 ADA acquisition, the product operates under ADA — a real continuity/roadmap risk for anyone evaluating 'Algonomy' today
The old 'landing page to cart' framing is no longer on the live page; the current site organizes the suite around named modules (Find, Recommend, Discover, Ensemble AI, Shopping Agent) instead
tools.bestFor: Retailers evaluating a full-funnel merchandising layer, with the caveat that the vendor relationship is now with ADA, not a standalone Algonomy.
questions: Where is the recs and ranking holdout?
What changes for existing Algonomy contracts now that ADA owns the product — same team, same roadmap?

tools.name: Athos Commerce
tools.summary: Athos Commerce is the January 2025 holding brand created when Searchspring and Klevu combined under PSG ownership, alongside Intelligent Reach — three separate products with separate contracts and pricing, not one merged platform.
strengths: Behavioral search re-ranking based on individual browsing and purchase history, plus segment-based category page reordering
Recommendations update in real time on browsing patterns, session behavior, and purchase history, with bundling capability
Personalization extends past on-site to email and SMS per the product page, wider than most pure on-site search/recs tools
limits: Confirmed, not just ambiguity: Klevu, Searchspring, and Intelligent Reach are sold as genuinely separate products with separate contracts, pricing, and integrations under the Athos Commerce parent brand — there is no single unified platform underneath despite the shared marketing site
Pricing is moving to quote-only 'Request Pricing,' reducing transparency even though the vendor says there's no change in pricing for the same features
Because it's genuinely three product lines, 'Athos Commerce personalization' as a single line item is misleading — confirm which underlying product (Klevu or Searchspring) is actually being quoted
tools.bestFor: Teams evaluating Klevu or Searchspring specifically, who should treat 'Athos Commerce' as the parent brand, not a unified product to diligence as one thing.
questions: Which underlying product — Klevu, Searchspring, or Intelligent Reach — is actually being scoped, and is the contract with that entity or with Athos?
Since it's not a merged platform, does personalization data (search behavior, purchase history) actually share across the underlying products, or is each siloed?

source.claim: Delivers one-to-one experiences across search, categories, product recommendations, email, and SMS; the site's footer still separately links to Klevu and Intelligent Reach logins, confirming separate underlying products.

library.name: Goal-first first screen
library.summary: The next page is built around the job they just named.
library.body: A quiz, a picker, or a search is a sentence. The following screen should answer it. Keep a path back to browse. Test against the default home.

library.name: Intent-weighted search ranking
library.summary: Results respect the query, then history — not the other way around.
library.body: Hold out default ranking. Measure search-to-product, not 'engagement'. Null searches are opportunities, not dead ends.

library.name: Campaign message match
library.summary: The page keeps the promise the ad made.
library.body: Cluster creatives, don't build 400 landing pages. Never apply campaign framing to people who typed your brand name.

library.name: Account-aware homepage
library.summary: Proof and CTA that match company size or industry.
library.body: Always offer 'not your company?'. Wrong ID is worse than the average page. Hold out a slice of target accounts.

library.name: Recommended plan chooser
library.summary: Pricing helps them choose, instead of staring.
library.body: Repeat visitors to pricing need a reason, not a discount. Recommend with an explanation, and keep the full table visible.

library.name: Objection-aware product page
library.summary: Repeat viewers get proof, not pressure.
library.body: Surface returns, implementation, or 'who it's for' after a pattern of visits. Fire on repeat, not first glance.

library.name: Session-first recommendations
library.summary: This visit's job outranks last year's purchase.
library.body: Keep history as a small 'your usual' module. Don't wipe it — demote it. Watch staple reorder as a guardrail.

library.name: Inline job complement
library.summary: One missing piece, named, in the cart.
library.body: Complements complete the job in the basket. One item, a reason, easy to ignore. Watch checkout conversion, not just AOV.

library.name: Pick up where you left off
library.summary: Restore the search, the filter, the page.
library.body: Manners, not magic. Expire it. Offer start fresh. Don't restore a gift session onto a later personal visit.

library.name: Assembled reading path
library.summary: The next three pieces follow the thread they pulled.
library.body: Synthesis, not a popularity widget. Measure pipeline or conversion, not time-on-site.

library.name: First-step empty state
library.summary: After pay, one useful action — not a product tour.
library.body: Name the first outcome they bought. Skip must work. Measure first-value, not tour completion.

library.name: Resume the unfinished step
library.summary: Stalled setup gets the next step, then silence.
library.body: One message, the actual step, a later option. Don't restart the tour. Don't drip for two weeks.

library.name: Help after repeated failure
library.summary: The same error three times is a product problem wearing a person's face.
library.body: Alternate path, clearer error, or a human. Log it. If a cohort fails, fix the step.

library.name: Offer the unused shorter path
library.summary: Prompt at the workaround, not in a global upsell.
library.body: Wait for a pattern. Show the job, then the plan. Let them say they already use something else.

library.name: Cadence-aware reorder
library.summary: Remind them when the pattern says they will need it.
library.body: Don't invent a cycle from two orders. Skip and pause must work. Optional subscribe, never surprise.

library.name: Save one useful default
library.summary: Ask to remember a size, a plan, a store — after it helped.
library.body: One field, in the moment of success. Show what you stored. Let them delete it.

library.name: Quiet usage check-in
library.summary: Decline vs their own baseline, not vs your whales.
library.body: Hypothesis, holdout, light touch. Ask what changed before you discount. Never lead with surveillance language.

library.name: Recover a dead search
library.summary: They told you what they wanted. Don't show a dead end.
library.body: Null search is a declared job. Close match, synonym, or nearest in-stock — named as such. Hold out the empty state. Bestsellers that ignore the query are not recovery.

library.name: Name the cart they left
library.summary: One reminder of the actual items. Discount last, not first.
library.body: Intervention, not a newsletter. Name the items, give a real stock or delivery reason, hold out. Three cart emails in three days is crowding.

library.name: Save after they name why
library.summary: Cancel stays one tap. The save comes after the reason.
library.body: Declared churn is the cleanest intervention signal you will get. A real pause, a real skip, a real question. Making cancel hard is a trap, not personalization.

library.name: Member-first first screen
library.summary: Reorder and benefits first. The catalog is still one tap away.
library.body: You already did the identity work. Serving a member the stranger homepage is wasted recognition. Don't lock them to last year's basket.

library.name: Three-intent treatment inside one test
library.summary: Low: stay out of the way. Medium: a nudge. High: go all in.
library.body: All visitors, same page. A is the default. B is one variant with three arms. Learn, then decide. Personalization does not get its own definition of proof.

library.name: Nobody is average
library.summary: Designing for the mean person designs for no one in particular.
library.body: The average customer is a spreadsheet artifact. Real people arrive with a job, a history, and a mood. Specificity is how you stop shipping the compromise.

library.name: Declared, connected, inferred
library.summary: Three kinds of evidence. They are not equally honest.
library.body: Declared is what they told you. Connected is what you already know. Inferred is a guess with manners. Start with declared. Treat inferred as a hypothesis.

library.name: Specificity has to earn its cost
library.summary: A different experience is more expensive. It needs a reason.
library.body: Every extra version is design, QA, measurement, and risk. If you cannot say what it is worth, you are collecting audiences as a hobby.

library.name: Not 'what can we build?'
library.summary: Start with what you should do, for whom, and why.
library.body: Old: buy a tool, then hunt for a use case. New: a real customer situation, then a tool if the reasoning holds. The decision record comes before the vendor.

library.name: Personalization runs inside experimentation
library.summary: No private intake. No private definition of proof.
library.body: Score, match, and serve sit between Intake and Decide. A personalized experience is a test: it enters at Intake, it is priced on the same goal tree, and it is killed at Decide if it does not pay.

library.name: The default is the control
library.summary: If everyone is 'personalized', you learned nothing.
library.body: A is the common experience. B is the specific treatment. Holdouts are how you stay honest when the algorithm wants to 'optimize' the whole site.

library.name: Three intent arms
library.summary: Stay out of the way, offer a nudge, or go all in.
library.body: The same situation does not deserve the same volume. Low-intent visitors should barely notice you. High-intent visitors can handle a full path. Medium is a single useful offer.

library.name: The decision record
library.summary: Who, why, what, how we'll know — written down.
library.body: If it isn't recorded, it cannot compound. The next team should not have to rediscover why this audience got this treatment.

library.name: Learning memory
library.summary: The compounding asset is the record, not the tool.
library.body: Research, experiments, and personalization write to the same memory. Treatments that worked, for whom, under which conditions, and why. It survives a team change.

library.name: Goal tree
library.summary: Nothing runs without a reason on the tree.
library.body: Outcomes cascade into metrics. Personalization adds audience and context nodes to the same tree. If you cannot point to a node, you cannot price the work.

library.name: Price the difference
library.summary: What is treating this audience differently actually worth?
library.body: Traffic, base rates, value per conversion. Personalization is sized as incremental value over the default — not as 'we launched 40 campaigns'.

library.name: Score, match, serve
library.summary: The POS loop, held inside the governor.
library.body: Score the situation. Match a treatment. Serve it as a test. Then Decide. It is a discipline, not a second operating system.

library.name: Demand is lowest at first purchase
library.summary: Customers care more in discovery, repurchase, and loyalty.
library.body: About 52% call personalization important at first purchase — the stage where almost every budget goes. Awareness, consideration, repurchase, and loyalty sit in the 60s. Put the work where they asked.

library.name: Not a software project
library.summary: The usual stall is people, integration, and creative speed.
library.body: 71% cite a siloed operating model. 59% a limited or unintegrated stack. 56% creative speed. Almost nobody cites 'we lacked a personalization tool'.

library.name: Holdouts
library.summary: A group that keeps the default, on purpose.
library.body: Without a holdout, every win is a story. With one, you can kill what doesn't pay. Holdouts are how personalization stays inside experimentation.

library.name: Affinity
library.summary: A tendency, not an identity.
library.body: Affinity is useful as a prior. It becomes harmful when it locks someone to last year's self. Session need can — and should — outrank it.

library.name: Proportionate response
library.summary: The volume of the experience should match the strength of the evidence.
library.body: A declared goal can change the first screen. An inferred churn score should not. Mismatch is how personalization gets a reputation.

library.name: Dismissible by default
library.summary: If they cannot avoid it, it is not a service.
library.body: Skip, not now, start fresh, not my company, don't show again. These are not edge cases. They are how you keep the right to be specific.

library.name: Reliable recognition
library.summary: If you cannot tell who they are, you cannot treat them differently.
library.body: Recognition is identity, a cookie, a campaign, a login — something stable enough to measure. Guessing loudly is worse than the default.

library.name: Enough eligible traffic
library.summary: A tiny audience cannot prove a tiny lift.
library.body: Judge the treatment on the people who would actually see it, not on site-wide sessions. If you cannot learn in a business cycle, sequence something else first.

library.name: Privacy and experience guardrails
library.summary: Consent, suppression, and 'don't be weird'.
library.body: Suppression lists, frequency caps, sensitive categories, shared devices. Personalization that ignores these is not bold. It is unpaid reputation risk.

library.name: First value, not first login
library.summary: Activation is the first useful outcome, not an account create.
library.body: Measure the event that means the product became real. Tours, emails sent, and 'engagement' are substitutes.

library.name: The job in front of them
library.summary: Treat the current job, not the lifetime profile.
library.body: Profiles are priors. The session is the plot. Complements, restored searches, and goal-first screens all respect the job in front of them.

library.name: Siloed handoffs
library.summary: The most named blocker is not the stack.
library.body: Research, marketing, product, and engineering passing a campaign over the wall is how programs stall. Personalization needs one backlog and one Decide.

library.name: AI made scale cheap
library.summary: It also made personalization attainable. Using it only for scale gets you commoditized.
library.body: Generation without a decision record is more average, faster. AI belongs after the situation is clear: to draft variants, not to pick the audience in the dark.

library.name: The leaders' gap
library.summary: About 10 points faster growth. Roughly $2T shifting this decade.
library.body: Most companies fail to capture it because they buy tools and recommendations instead of proving where specificity is worth the cost. Source: BCG, restated in HBR, Nov 2024.

library.name: Seven questions before anything ships
library.summary: A single no sends it back.
library.body: Relevant? Current? Easier? Understandable? Proportionate? Dismissible? Learnable? Clearing a decision record is not the last check.

library.name: Write the decision record first
library.summary: The tool gets picked after, not before.
library.body: Situation, audience, signals, treatment, measure, owner. If you cannot fill it, you are not ready to configure a campaign.

library.name: Test against the default
library.summary: Personalization is a variant, not a new religion.
library.body: Same page, same metric, a holdout. If it cannot beat the common experience, it does not ship to 100%.

library.name: Start where intent is clear and change is easy
library.summary: High intent, high ability to change the experience.
library.body: Queue high-intent/hard-to-change work. Use easy/weaker-signal tests to build evidence. Deprioritize weak signal and hard change.

library.name: Measure the people who would see it
library.summary: Site-wide traffic is a vanity denominator.
library.body: Judge the treatment on the people who would actually see it. If that slice is too small to learn from, pick another situation.

library.name: One complement, not three carousels
library.summary: Useful is narrower than 'also like'.
library.body: Name the missing piece of the job. Put it next to the thing it completes. Make it ignorable. Watch checkout, not just attach rate.

library.name: Skip must work
library.summary: Tours, restores, and account swaps need an exit.
library.body: If skip is hidden, you will train people to distrust the next specific experience. Measure skip. It is a signal.

library.name: Wait for a pattern
library.summary: Once is a moment. Twice is a situation.
library.body: Don't prompt on the first export, the first pricing view, or the first decline. Patterns are how you stay proportionate.

library.name: Say why they got it
library.summary: Mystery rearranges feel like surveillance.
library.body: 'Because you searched X.' 'Because you told us you are on a team of 12.' If you cannot say it out loud, don't ship it.

library.name: Write the kill criteria
library.summary: Campaigns without an off switch become the site.
library.body: Guardrail, date, or 'if skip > X'. Decide is a real meeting. Personalization does not get to live forever because it launched.

library.name: Pick the tool last
library.summary: The record chooses the application, then the tool.
library.body: Map the situation to an application, then to a stack role, then to a vendor you already run if you can. Buying first is how programs stall.

library.name: Same backlog as experiments
library.summary: If personalization has a side door, it will skip Decide.
library.body: Intake, pricing, and readout live with the rest of XOS. A 'growth hack' channel is how you get 40 overlapping campaigns on one page.

library.name: If a cohort fails, fix the step
library.summary: Don't personalize around a broken onboarding field.
library.body: Repeated errors are product work. Help is the treatment while you fix it. Targeting is not a patch on a bug.

library.name: Compare people to themselves
library.summary: Decline vs their baseline, not vs power users.
library.body: Inferred churn that uses whales as the norm will nag your quiet-but-healthy customers. Quiet check-ins only earn the right to exist if the baseline is theirs.

myths.claim: Personalization means putting their name in the email.
myths.truth: It means changing the experience because their situation is different.
myths.detail: A mail merge is a greeting. Personalization is a decision: which experience, for whom, under which conditions, from signals you already have. If the page is the same, the name in the subject line did not count.

myths.claim: We need a personalization platform before we can start.
myths.truth: Most stalls are people, integration, and creative speed — not a missing SKU.
myths.detail: BCG's Personalization Index: 71% cite a siloed operating model, 59% a limited or unintegrated stack, 56% the speed of creative. Personalization gets run as a software project. It is a relationship, governed like any other test.

myths.claim: The money is in converting the first purchase.
myths.truth: That is the stage where customers care least.
myths.detail: Share who call personalization important: awareness 62%, consideration 65%, first purchase 52%, repurchase 64%, loyalty 62%. The first-purchase budget is a habit. Demand is in discovery, repurchase, and loyalty. Source: Abraham & Edelman, Personalized (HBR Press, 2024).

myths.claim: More campaigns means we are more mature.
myths.truth: If everything is personalized, you cannot tell what paid.
myths.detail: Leaders' customers spend about 30% more and engage about 3× as often — not because they saw more popups, but because specificity was proven. A default holdout is how you stay in the second group.

myths.claim: If we get specific, it will feel creepy.
myths.truth: Creepy is mystery. Specific and explained is service.
myths.detail: Say why they got it. Make it dismissible. Keep inferred signals quieter than declared ones. The seven questions exist so you don't ship the version that feels like surveillance.

myths.truth: AI made scale cheap. It did not make the decision for you.
myths.detail: Brands that use AI only to produce more average, faster, get commoditized. Use it after the situation is clear: to draft a variant, not to invent an audience in the dark. The decision record still comes first.

myths.truth: You probably have the three kinds. The experience doesn't use them.
myths.detail: What someone tells you, what you already know, and what their behavior suggests: most companies collect all three. The question isn't whether the data exists. It's whether the experience reflects it.

myths.claim: Once it's on, we should leave it on.
myths.truth: A personalized experience is a test. Tests get killed.
myths.detail: It enters at Intake, it is priced on the same goal tree, and it is killed at Decide if it does not pay. Personalization gets no governance of its own. It uses the experimentation operating system's.

roadmap.detail: Goals, constraints, owners. What 'good' would look like in numbers you already track.

roadmap.name: Maturity audit
roadmap.detail: A scored baseline: people, stack, and how decisions actually get made.

roadmap.name: Ingest audience insight
roadmap.detail: Prior research into memory, so the first personalizations don't start from zero.

roadmap.name: Existing signals scan
roadmap.detail: What data you can already act on — declared, connected, inferred.

roadmap.name: High-value use case
roadmap.detail: One case, sized and scoped. Designed as a variant against the default.

roadmap.detail: A sequenced, priced plan — and a decision point on whether to continue.
